claims.claim: The Q-matrix is a binary item-by-attribute incidence matrix: a 1 where an attribute (skill) is needed to solve the item, a 0 where it is not. It is attributed to Tatsuoka's rule-space work, which modelled misconceptions in fraction arithmetic. It is the standard way to say 'this question judges these skills', and every model below takes it as input.
claims.source: Tatsuoka, K. K. (1983). Rule space: An approach for dealing with misconceptions based on item response theory. Journal of Educational Measurement 20(4), 345-354
claims.relevance: For Fluenough this is a question-type by skill matrix. Example rows: chooseMeaning = {Recognition}, hearMeaning = {Hear, Recognition}, speak = {Say, recall-production}, cloze-typed = {Write, Grammar?}. Write it down explicitly instead of crediting one skill per question type. Secondary sources say other works share credit for the Q-matrix, so do not claim Tatsuoka 1983 invented it.

claims.claim: DINA (deterministic input, noisy AND) is conjunctive: to answer correctly a learner must have mastered ALL the attributes the Q-matrix lists for the item, apart from a slip parameter and a guess parameter. A failure is therefore evidence that at least one required skill is missing.
claims.source: Junker, B. W. & Sijtsma, K. (2001). Cognitive assessment models with few assumptions, and connections with nonparametric item response theory. Applied Psychological Measurement 25(3), 258-272
claims.numbers: 2 parameters per item (slip, guess)
claims.relevance: Fits the questions where every listed skill is needed, e.g. dictation or hear-and-type, which need both hearing and spelling. A wrong answer should spread blame across skills, not put full blame on each one.

claims.claim: DINO (deterministic input, noisy OR) is the compensatory counterpart: one mastered required attribute is enough to answer correctly. It still has only a guess and a slip parameter per item, however many attributes there are.
claims.source: Templin, J. L. & Henson, R. A. (2006). Measurement of psychological disorders using cognitive diagnosis models. Psychological Methods 11(3), 287-305
claims.relevance: Fits questions that can be solved through any of several routes, e.g. a meaning question answerable by sound OR by spelling. Under OR logic a success says little about any single skill, so credit per skill should be small.

claims.claim: The Additive Factors Model (AFM), used in Learning Factors Analysis, generalises the Rasch model to learning over time. Success can depend on several skills, linked to items through a Q-matrix. In the standard formulation, the logit adds student ability plus, for EACH skill the item requires, that skill's easiness and its learning rate times the number of prior opportunities. Credit is compensatory and additive, and every tagged skill gets a full practice opportunity.
claims.source: Cen, H., Koedinger, K. & Junker, B. (2006). Learning Factors Analysis - A general method for cognitive model evaluation and improvement. ITS 2006, LNCS 4053, 164-175 (Springer)
claims.relevance: In AFM, one answer increments the opportunity count of every skill in the item, each with its own learning rate. This is the simplest principled replacement for one global .68 weight: a separate gain per (question type, skill) pair, fitted from data.

claims.claim: Performance Factors Analysis (PFA) adapts AFM for adaptive practice. It counts prior successes and prior failures separately per skill, with separate weights, and sums over all the skills tagged to the item. The authors say it was motivated partly because knowledge tracing 'has not been used to capture learning where multiple skills are needed to perform a single action'.
claims.source: Pavlik, P. I., Cen, H. & Koedinger, K. R. (2009). Performance Factors Analysis - A new alternative to knowledge tracing. AIED 2009, 531-538 (IOS Press)
claims.relevance: Separate success and failure weights per skill match the owner's point that one skill partly implies another. A correct Say answer may say a lot about Recognition, while a failed Say says little about Recognition. The weights in the two directions should differ.

claims.claim: Gong, Beck & Heffernan's journal version compares models on predicting individual student practice opportunities. It finds that PFA has considerably higher predictive accuracy than knowledge tracing, with more plausible parameters. Treatment of multi-skill items is one of the design choices compared, but I could not open the text to check how multi-skill items were handled.
claims.source: Gong, Y., Beck, J. E. & Heffernan, N. T. (2011). How to construct more accurate student models: Comparing and optimizing knowledge tracing and performance factor analysis. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education 21(1-2), 27-46
claims.relevance: Supports a logistic, additive, multi-skill model (PFA/AFM style) over separate per-skill binary trackers. This is relevant to Fluenough's Elo layer, which is logistic.

claims.claim: Conjunctive knowledge tracing addresses blame assignment. When several knowledge components are needed for one correct step, the simple update lowers ALL of them after an error even though only one may be to blame. In tutor logs this caused 'problem selection thrashing'. Applied to those logs, a conjunctive (Bayes-net) update suggests that about a third of assigned problems may have been unnecessary.
claims.source: Koedinger, K. R., Pavlik, P. I., Stamper, J., Nixon, T. & Ritter, S. (2011). Avoiding problem selection thrashing with conjunctive knowledge tracing. EDM 2011, 91-100
claims.numbers: 441 of 1370 problems (about one third) possibly unnecessary
claims.relevance: This is a direct warning for a fixed cross-skill weight on failures. If a failed hear-and-type question lowers Hear AND Write at full weight, the scheduler may keep resurfacing a skill that is fine. Split blame in proportion to how likely each skill is to be the cause.

claims.claim: Knowledge Tracing Machines (factorization machines) contain AFM, PFA and multidimensional IRT as special cases. They handle side information such as multiple knowledge components per item and attempt counts at item or skill level. They estimate knowledge accurately even when data is sparse, on real datasets with tens of thousands of users and items.
claims.source: Vie, J.-J. & Kashima, H. (2019). Knowledge Tracing Machines: Factorization machines for knowledge tracing. AAAI-19, 33(01), 750-757
claims.population: Several public education datasets (math tutors, etc.)
claims.relevance: KTM is the general frame: the features of one answer are the word, each skill it touches and per-skill win/fail counts, and an FM learns interactions between them, including skill-skill transfer. It is a fitting target once Fluenough has review logs.

claims.claim: In an independent benchmark (ASSIST2009, Algebra06, EdNet), DAS3H AUC was 0.785 / 0.793 / 0.731 and KTM 0.792 / 0.794 / 0.730. AFM was much lower at 0.624 / 0.699 / 0.641. The search summary noted that the table's headers were partly garbled when extracted.
claims.source: Zhang, M., Zhu, X., Zhang, C., Ji, Y., Pan, F. & Yin, C. (2021). Multi-Factors Aware Dual-Attentional Knowledge Tracing. CIKM 2021 (arXiv 2108.04741)
claims.relevance: Multi-skill models that also track time and per-item difficulty clearly beat additive skill-only models. Per-(word, skill) difficulty plus per-skill ability plus time is the right shape.

claims.claim: DAS3H combines item difficulty, student ability, and per-skill learning and forgetting. For each skill an item involves, it counts past attempts and wins in several time windows, so learning and forgetting curves can differ by skill. A multi-skill item's logit sums these terms over all its skills. The authors state that no earlier knowledge tracing model handled both memory decay and multiple skill tagging. The model beat other state-of-the-art EDM models on 3 real datasets and won the EDM 2019 best full paper award.
claims.source: Choffin, B., Popineau, F., Bourda, Y. & Vie, J.-J. (2019). DAS3H: Modeling student learning and forgetting for optimally scheduling distributed practice of skills. EDM 2019 (arXiv 1905.06873)
claims.numbers: Repo-reported AUC 0.826 +/- 0.003 (Algebra 2005-06), 0.790 +/- 0.004 (Bridge to Algebra 2006-07); window lengths (I recall 1/24, 1, 7, 30 days and all time) not verified
claims.population: Algebra 2005-06, Bridge to Algebra 2006-07 (KDD Cup), ASSISTments 2012 (US math)
claims.relevance: This is the closest published analogue to Fluenough: one answer updates several skills' memory traces, and each skill has its own forgetting. It argues for per-skill FSRS stability updates from multi-skill questions, with a decay per skill, e.g. Say may fade faster than Recognition.

claims.claim: Choffin et al. adapt three spacing heuristics to choose which skill to review, and add a multi-skill heuristic that picks the most promising SUBSET of skills. In simulation (cohorts of 500 simulated students) the subset choice gave better retention than choosing only the single best skill.
claims.source: Choffin, B., Popineau, F. & Bourda, Y. (2021). Extending adaptive spacing heuristics to multi-skill items. Journal of Educational Data Mining 13(3), 69-102
claims.numbers: 500 simulated students per cohort; no effect size retrieved
claims.relevance: Supports scheduling question types that exercise several due skills of a word at once, e.g. a hear-and-type question covering due Hear and Write. Evidence is simulated only.

claims.claim: Multidimensional Elo (M-ERS) builds a compensatory multidimensional IRT model into Elo. One response updates SEVERAL ability parameters at once, weighted by the item's loadings on each dimension (Q-matrix with weights). In simulations, unidimensional Elo had much lower prediction accuracy than M-ERS when the data were multidimensional. Adding response speed improved it further.
claims.source: Park, J. Y., Cornillie, F., van der Maas, H. L. J. & Van Den Noortgate, W. (2019). A multidimensional IRT approach for dynamically monitoring ability growth in computerized practice environments. Frontiers in Psychology 10:620
claims.numbers: 3 simulation studies; no exact accuracy figures retrieved
claims.population: Simulation plus real data from a math practice platform (not language)
claims.relevance: This is the principled form of Fluenough's Elo cross-skill update. Instead of one .68 for every pair, each question type gets a loading vector over skills (e.g. hearMeaning: Hear 1.0, Recognition 0.5), and the Elo error is shared out by those loadings.

claims.claim: M-Elo (Abdi et al.) keeps a separate rating per concept for items tagged with one or more concepts. It beats plain Elo as learners' abilities across concepts become more diverse, i.e. as the simulation's sigma rises. A 2025 comparison found M-Elo converges faster but shows significant bias and lower prediction accuracy than M-ERS. M-ERS was robust to misspecification of the Q-matrix and its weights.
claims.source: Abdi, S., Khosravi, H., Sadiq, S. & Gasevic, D. (2019). A multivariate Elo-based learner model for adaptive educational systems. EDM 2019 (arXiv 1910.12581); Vermeiren, Hofman & Bolsinova (2025). Evaluating multidimensional extensions of the Elo rating systems for tracking ability in online learning environments. EDM 2025
claims.relevance: If Fluenough's skills really differ per learner (e.g. strong reader, weak listener), per-skill ratings are worth having. A weighted compensatory update (M-ERS) is preferable to splitting the update evenly. Robustness to a wrong Q-matrix matters because the weights will be hand-set at first.

claims.claim: On geography-fact data (prior knowledge), basic Elo gave good prediction accuracy. A hierarchical model and a networked model (multivariate Elo, in which an answer on one item also updates related items) improved predictions only slightly. Their main value was information about learners and the domain.
claims.source: Nižnan, J., Pelánek, R. & Řihák, J. (2015). Student models for prior knowledge estimation. EDM 2015, 109-116
claims.numbers: 'only slightly' better; exact figures not retrieved
claims.population: Users of an adaptive geography practice system (Czech, outlinemaps.org)
claims.relevance: Spreading credit to related items across items within a skill tends to give small accuracy gains. Do not expect large gains from the cross-skill layer. Validate it on logs before treating it as the backbone.

claims.claim: Half-life regression (HLR) estimates each word's memory half-life from features of the learner's history and lexeme tag features (word difficulty). It cut error by 45%+ over baselines at predicting recall. Each lexeme is a separate indicator feature (in the released data, a lemma with its POS and morphology), so there is no explicit credit-sharing across skills or forms. Exercise formats are pooled into one recall trace.
claims.source: Settles, B. & Meeder, B. (2016). A trainable spaced repetition model for language learning. ACL 2016, 1848-1858
claims.numbers: 45%+ error reduction vs baselines; about 13M learning traces
claims.relevance: Duolingo's published scheduler does NOT split credit per skill. Different formats all count as exposures of one lexeme. Fluenough's per-skill FSRS plus cross-skill transfer goes beyond HLR, and the size of the transfer has no HLR evidence behind it. The lexeme-level detail is my recollection of the dataset (Medium).

claims.claim: The Duolingo SLAM corpus has token-level errors for over 6k learners (English, Spanish, French tracks, more than 7M words). Exercise format is a feature of each item. The logistic regression baseline reached AUC .774 on English. The best system reached AUC .861.
claims.source: Settles, B., Brust, C., Gustafson, E., Hagiwara, M. & Madnani, N. (2018). Second language acquisition modeling. BEA Workshop at NAACL 2018, 56-65
claims.numbers: baseline AUC .774 (en); top AUC .861; 15 teams
claims.population: Duolingo learners of English (from Spanish), Spanish and French (from English)
claims.relevance: This is a public dataset where the same word appears in different formats (I believe reverse_translate, reverse_tap, listen; field names not verified). It could be used to estimate how much success in one format predicts another for the same word, i.e. empirical cross-skill weights.

claims.claim: Fractional Implicit Repetition (FIRe) at Math Academy: practising an advanced topic gives discounted ('fractional') implicit repetition credit to the simpler topics it contains. The credit trickles down the knowledge graph, and choosing reviews that clear other due reviews ('repetition compression') reduces review load. I found no independent or peer-reviewed evaluation.
claims.source: Skycak, J. (2023 approx.). Optimized, individualized spaced repetition in hierarchical knowledge structures (blog; The Math Academy Way, draft). Not peer-reviewed
claims.numbers: none published
claims.relevance: This is the nearest SRS analogue to 'one skill partially implies others'. A production skill (Say/Write) passed early could give fractional FSRS credit to the receptive skills (Recognition/Hear). It is a design precedent only, not evidence. I could not read the page (proxy blocked) to report its weights.

claims.claim: A controlled study asked whether retrieval practice of translations in one direction transfers to the other. Across 3 experiments, learners practised receptively (L2 to English) or productively (English to L2) to a criterion of 3 correct recalls, then practised the opposite direction. I could not retrieve which direction transferred more, or by how much.
claims.source: Bernardi, Vaughn, Dunlosky & Rawson (2024). Toward mastering foreign-language translations: transfer between productive and receptive learning. Memory (PMID 39222444)
claims.numbers: not retrieved
claims.population: English-speaking adults learning foreign-language translations (likely Swahili or similar; not verified)
claims.relevance: This is the direct empirical source for asymmetric transfer between Recognition and Say/Write. Read the full text to get the trials-to-criterion savings and use them as the cross-skill weight in each direction.

claims.claim: Anki's 'siblings' (cards generated from the same note, such as front-to-back and back-to-front) are not given shared credit. The option only buries siblings for the day to avoid interference. There is no peer-reviewed source for this; it is Anki's documentation and my inference.
claims.source: Anki Manual (documentation, not peer-reviewed)
claims.relevance: FSRS as deployed in Anki schedules each direction independently. So Fluenough's cross-skill transfer is an extension beyond FSRS and has to be validated by Fluenough itself.

gaps: Full texts could not be opened: the egress proxy blocked arxiv.org, aclanthology.org, educationaldatamining.org, fi.muni.cz, justinmath.com and others. Claims come from abstracts and search summaries. Exact update equations were not read in the papers themselves: DAS3H time windows, the M-ERS weighting formula, M-Elo's split rule and FIRe's discount fractions.

I found no peer-reviewed study that fits cross-skill weights between receptive, aural and productive word skills inside an SRS or Elo system. The .68 weight (Milton & Hopkins 2006) is a correlation between vocabulary SIZES across learners. It is not a within-word transfer rate per item, and using it as an update weight is an inference.
Pelánek's own multi-concept Elo variants (e.g. UMUAI 2017 overview; Computers & Education 2016) may treat multi-KC items, but I could not confirm how.
Bernardi et al. 2024 transfer numbers (receptive vs productive) were not retrieved, and they are the most directly useful figures.

No head-to-head DAS3H vs single-skill DAS3H on language data was found. Zylich & Lan 'Linguistic skill modeling for SLA' (LAK 2021) and Ma et al. 'Each encounter counts' (LAK 2023) exist but their results were not retrieved.

I found no source evaluating asymmetric credit, i.e. a success giving credit to other skills while a failure spreads little blame. It is supported only indirectly by PFA's separate success/failure weights and by Koedinger et al. 2011 on blame.

Recommended next step: once logs exist, fit a PFA/KTM-style model with per-(question type, skill) Q-matrix weights. Alternatively, estimate cross-format transfer on the public Duolingo SLAM data, instead of using a single literature weight.

checked.claim: Q-matrix is a binary item-by-attribute matrix attributed to Tatsuoka's rule-space work, which modelled misconceptions in fraction arithmetic
checked.source: Tatsuoka, K. K. (1983). Rule space. Journal of Educational Measurement 20(4), 345-354
checked.correction: The citation is correct: JEM 20(4), 345-354. The 1983 abstract describes rule space as a way to classify misconceptions by combining IRT with Lee's (1983) algebraic database theory. The fraction work is mainly in Tatsuoka's 1984 technical report on fraction addition and subtraction (20 items, 536 middle-school students) and in later papers such as 'Bug distribution and statistical pattern classification' (Psychometrika, 1987), which uses fraction arithmetic. I could not confirm that the 1983 article itself uses fractions or prints a Q-matrix. The standard 20x8 fraction-subtraction Q-matrix comes from the 1984 data, as reproduced by de la Torre & Douglas (2004) and DeCarlo (2011). Cite Tatsuoka 1983 for rule space and the 1984 report for the fraction Q-matrix. Confidence: Medium (secondary sources only).

checked.claim: DINA is conjunctive: all required attributes are needed, apart from one slip and one guess parameter per item
checked.source: Junker & Sijtsma (2001). Applied Psychological Measurement 25(3), 258-272
checked.correction: The citation is correct. The abstract describes a 'stochastic conjunctive relationship' between attributes and task performance. Secondary sources (GDINA manual, CDM texts) confirm that DINA has only two parameters per item, whatever the number of attributes K. Medium for the parameter count, from secondary sources. The Fluenough inference that a failure should spread blame across skills is the claimant's own.

checked.claim: DINO (noisy OR) is the compensatory counterpart with guess/slip per item; illustrated on pathological gamblers
checked.source: Templin & Henson (2006). Psychological Methods 11(3), 287-305
checked.correction: The citation and DOI are correct. The abstract introduces DINO ('deterministic input, noisy or gate') and illustrates it by diagnosing pathological gamblers against the DSM-IV-TR criteria. The two parameters per item (guess and slip) are a standard secondary description; the abstract I saw does not state it. Medium.

checked.claim: AFM/LFA: logit = student ability + sum over Q-matrix skills of (easiness + learning rate x prior opportunities); geometry tutor data
checked.source: Cen, Koedinger & Junker (2006). ITS 2006, LNCS 4053, 164-175
checked.correction: The citation and pages are correct. The abstract describes LFA as combining a statistical model, human expertise and combinatorial search. I could not read the AFM equation in the text, so the formula and the geometry dataset are confirmed only from secondary knowledge (Medium). Note that the abstract presents LFA as a method for evaluating cognitive models. AFM is its statistical component.

checked.claim: PFA counts prior successes and failures per skill; motivated because KT 'has not been used to capture learning where multiple skills are needed to perform a single action'
checked.source: Pavlik, Cen & Koedinger (2009). AIED 2009, 531-538, IOS Press
checked.correction: The quote appears verbatim in the abstract. The abstract also describes 'a logistic regression equation that models changes in performance in terms of the number of student successes and failures ... for each skill'. The canonical record is DOI 10.3233/978-1-60750-028-5-531. I could not verify the ERIC ID ED506305; a better repository link is digitalcommons.memphis.edu/facpubs/8350. The population (Cognitive Tutor algebra/geometry) was not verified. The claimant's Say/Recognition example is inference.

checked.claim: Gong, Beck & Heffernan 2011: PFA has considerably higher predictive accuracy than KT, with more plausible parameters; ASSISTments
checked.source: Gong, Beck & Heffernan (2011). IJAIED 21(1-2), 27-46
checked.correction: The abstract states that PFA 'has considerably higher predictive accuracy than KT' and that its 'parameter estimates were more plausible'. On multi-skill items, a summary of the issue (not the abstract) reports that the best model was a PFA variant that ignored the tutor's transfer model, i.e. it assumed every skill affects every problem. That is relevant: a hand-made Q-matrix was not the best performer. I did not verify the page numbers 27-46. Medium for the multi-skill detail.

checked.claim: Conjunctive KT avoids problem selection thrashing; 441 of 1370 problems possibly unnecessary
checked.source: Koedinger, Pavlik, Stamper, Nixon & Ritter (2011). EDM 2011, 91-100
checked.correction: The abstract confirms the claim: a simple update lowers all knowledge components (KCs) after an error, thrashing was seen in tutor logs, and the conjunctive (Bayes-net and psychometrics) approach suggests that 441 of 1,370 assigned problems may have been unnecessary. The 'math' population was not verified from the abstract.

checked.claim: Knowledge Tracing Machines subsume AFM, PFA, MIRT; handle multiple KCs and attempt counts; accurate on sparse data with tens of thousands of users and items
checked.correction: The abstract confirms all of this: factorization machines contain several existing educational models as special cases, they handle side information such as multiple knowledge components and attempt counts, and they estimate knowledge accurately and quickly with sparse data on real datasets of tens of thousands of users and items. arXiv: 1811.03388.

checked.source: Zhang et al. (2021). CIKM 2021, arXiv 2108.04741
checked.correction: Table 2, as extracted from search, gives exactly these AUCs (ASSIST2009 / Algebra06 / EdNet): AFM .624/.699/.641, PFA .705/.741/.655, KTM .792/.794/.730, DAS3H .785/.793/.731, MF-DAKT .851/.844/.776. The EdNet column header was garbled in extraction. The paper's text gives KTM on EdNet as 73.1%, so KTM and DAS3H may be swapped in that column. All baselines were run by the MF-DAKT authors, and the dataset statistics differ from other papers. DOI 10.1145/3459637.3482372. Caveat: KTM and DAS3H beat AFM by a lot, but they are within about 0.01 AUC of each other, so the time-window features add little over KTM here. That weakens the conclusion that time 'clearly' helps.

checked.claim: DAS3H: item difficulty, ability, per-skill learning/forgetting over time windows; no earlier KT model handled both memory decay and multiple skill tagging; beat SOTA on 3 datasets; EDM 2019 best full paper; repo AUC 0.826/0.790; windows 1/24,1,7,30,inf
checked.source: Choffin, Popineau, Bourda & Vie (2019). EDM 2019, arXiv 1905.06873
checked.correction: The abstract confirms the model description, the sentence 'no knowledge tracing model takes both memory decay and multiple skill tagging into account', the 3 real datasets and the out-performance claim. The EDM 2019 awards page and a RIKEN AIP notice confirm the Best (Full) Paper Award. I could NOT verify the repo-reported AUCs (0.826 ± 0.003 and 0.790 ± 0.004) or the window lengths (1/24, 1, 7, 30 days, all time), so treat those as unsupported until the GitHub README or Table 3 of the paper is read.

checked.claim: Choffin et al. 2021 extend spacing heuristics to multi-skill items; subset selection beats single best skill in simulation; 500 simulated students per cohort
checked.source: Choffin, Popineau & Bourda (2021). JEDM 13(3), 69-102
checked.correction: The paper exists (JEDM 13(3), 2021; HAL hal-03418179; JEDM article 510). The abstract confirms that three spacing heuristics were adapted, multi-skill variants that select a subset of skills were added for two of them (five heuristics in total), and in a simulation of learning and forgetting, a well-chosen subset gave better retention than the single best skill. I could NOT verify the '500 simulated students per cohort', the pages 69-102 or the Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.5634220. The canonical URL is https://jedm.educationaldatamining.org/index.php/JEDM/article/view/510.

checked.claim: M-ERS: compensatory MIRT in Elo, multiple abilities updated at once; unidimensional Elo much lower accuracy on multidimensional data; response speed helps further
checked.source: Park, Cornillie, van der Maas & Van Den Noortgate (2019). Frontiers in Psychology 10:620
checked.correction: The abstract confirms the claim: there were 3 simulation studies, the unidimensional version had 'seriously lower prediction accuracy' than M-ERS, and modelling response speed together with accuracy improved performance. The real data came from a popular platform for practising math skills. The abstract does not give exact accuracy figures.

checked.claim: M-Elo (Abdi 2019) beats plain Elo as abilities across concepts become more diverse (sigma rises); Vermeiren 2025: M-Elo converges faster but has significant bias and lower accuracy than M-ERS; M-ERS robust to Q-matrix misspecification
checked.source: Abdi, Khosravi, Sadiq & Gasevic (2019) EDM 2019 / arXiv 1910.12581; Vermeiren, Hofman & Bolsinova (2025) EDM 2025
checked.correction: The Vermeiren et al. 2025 part is confirmed by its abstract: MELO converges faster but 'exhibits significant bias and lower prediction accuracy' than MERS, MERS is robust to misspecification of the Q-matrix and its weights, and both beat unidimensional Elo on multidimensional data. The study used simulation only. For Abdi et al. 2019, the abstract says only that the model has superior predictive performance over standard Elo on synthetic and public data, 'but the difference is rather small'. I could NOT verify the claim that it wins more as sigma rises. Report the gain as small. Vermeiren 2025 URL: https://educationaldatamining.org/EDM2025/proceedings/2025.EDM.long-papers.99/index.html

checked.claim: On geography data basic Elo gave good accuracy; hierarchical and networked (multivariate Elo) models improved predictions only slightly; main value is information about students and domain
checked.source: Nizan, Pelanek & Rihak (2015). EDM 2015, 109-116
checked.correction: The abstract confirms the claim. It compares four models (Elo, a Bayesian extension of Elo, a hierarchical model, and a networked model, multivariate Elo) on data from a geography-learning application: basic Elo performs well and the complex models improve predictions 'only slightly', being more useful for insight into students and the domain. The repository lists the author order as Rihak, Pelanek, Niznan (Nižnan, Pelánek, Řihák in the claim's order), so check the PDF. No numbers are in the abstract.

checked.claim: HLR estimates per-word half-life from history and lexeme features; 45%+ error reduction; Duolingo; formats pooled, no cross-skill credit
checked.source: Settles & Meeder (2016). ACL 2016, 1848-1858
checked.correction: The abstract and the ACL Anthology confirm the citation, the pages, the Duolingo data and the '45%+' error reduction versus several baselines at predicting student recall rates. I did not verify the '13M learning traces' or the lexeme-tag and format-pooling details (Medium or Low). The statement that HLR has no cross-skill credit is the claimant's inference.

checked.claim: SLAM 2018: >6k learners, 3 tracks, >7M words; exercise format a feature; baseline AUC .774 (en); top AUC .861; 15 teams
checked.source: Settles, Brust, Gustafson, Hagiwara & Madnani (2018). BEA Workshop at NAACL 2018, 56-65
checked.correction: The citation, pages, 3 tracks and 15 teams are confirmed. Secondary papers confirm about 6.4k learners (en 2.6k, es 2.6k, fr 1.2k). Their token tables sum to about 7.1M (my arithmetic). They also confirm exercise formats reverse_translate, reverse_tap and listen as a per-exercise field, the English-track baseline AUC .774, and the English-track best AUC .861 (Spanish .835, French .854). The figures come from Vie 2018 (W18-0545), a Stanford report and a poster, not from the overview paper itself (Medium). The data covers each learner's first 30 days only.

checked.claim: FIRe at Math Academy: practising an advanced topic gives discounted implicit credit to the topics it contains; repetition compression; no peer-reviewed evaluation
checked.source: Skycak (blog; The Math Academy Way)
checked.correction: Skycak's post (search excerpt) confirms trickle-down implicit repetitions that are discounted ('fractional') and the selection of reviews that knock out other due reviews. No formula or weights are published in what I saw, and I found no peer-reviewed evaluation. This is a design precedent only, as the claimant says.

checked.claim: Bernardi et al. 2024: 3 experiments, receptive or productive practice to a criterion of 3 correct, then the opposite direction; direction and size of transfer not retrieved
checked.source: Bernardi, Vaughn, Dunlosky & Rawson (2024). Memory, PMID 39222444
checked.correction: The design is confirmed (3 experiments, dropout to 3 correct recalls, then the opposite direction to the same criterion). The abstract does give the headline result: across all experiments transfer was PARTIAL (practice in one direction did not remove the need to practise the other), and transfer occurred whichever direction came first. The abstract reports no clear asymmetry and no savings figures. Population and language (Swahili?) are not verified. The full text is needed for trials-to-criterion savings.

checked.claim: Anki siblings get no shared credit; burying only hides them for the day
checked.source: Anki Manual
checked.correction: The manual confirms that siblings are cards from the same note and that burying hides new or review siblings until the next day (learning cards are never buried), with separate options for new and review cards. The manual does not describe any shared scheduling credit, so 'no shared credit' is a reasonable inference (Low or Medium). The current URL is docs.ankiweb.net/studying.html.

claims.claim: Form-meaning knowledge has four strength levels that form a difficulty hierarchy: active recall (supply the L2 word from the meaning) is hardest, then passive recall (supply the meaning of the L2 word), then active recognition (pick the L2 word), then passive recognition (pick the meaning) is easiest. The abstract says the hierarchy held at every word-frequency level. The authors framed the levels as an implicational scale: knowing a word at a harder level implies knowing it at the easier ones.
claims.source: Laufer, B. & Goldstein, Z. (2004). Testing vocabulary knowledge: Size, strength, and computer adaptiveness. Language Learning 54(3), 399-436. DOI 10.1111/j.0023-8333.2004.00260.x
claims.numbers: N = 435 high-school and university EFL learners (secondary sources say mostly L1 Hebrew); 30 words per frequency band plus Academic Word List items. A secondary summary says passive recall had the highest correlation with L2 achievement (.65); not checked against the paper. Scale reproducibility and scalability coefficients not found.
claims.population: L2 English learners in Israel, mostly L1 Hebrew, high school and university
claims.relevance: This hierarchy is the main basis for asymmetric, directional transfer between skills. Mapped to app skills: typing the word (Write type, and Say) = active recall; chooseWord, cloze choose and rearrange = active recognition; recalled meaning (recognition self-rated reveal, hear-and-type meaning) = passive recall; chooseMeaning, matchPairs and hearMeaning = passive recognition. A pass at a harder level should raise the easier skills a lot. A pass at an easier level should raise the harder skills only a little. A fail at an easier level is strong evidence that the harder skills would fail too. One symmetric weight (.68) does not capture this.

claims.claim: Across four word-knowledge components (form-meaning link, derivatives, multiple meanings, collocations), recognition knowledge of every component came before recall knowledge of any component. Implicational scaling found a consistent order of acquisition, and the components were closely related to one another.
claims.source: González-Fernández, B. & Schmitt, N. (2020). Word knowledge: Exploring the relationships and order of acquisition of vocabulary knowledge components. Applied Linguistics 41(4), 481-505. DOI 10.1093/applin/amy057 (one secondary source gives amy052)
claims.numbers: N = 144 L1 Spanish learners of English; 8 measures (4 components x recognition/recall). Correlation values and scaling coefficients not retrieved (publisher page unreachable from this environment).
claims.population: Adult L1 Spanish EFL learners, mixed proficiency
claims.relevance: Supports a one-way rule: success in recall implies recognition, but recognition does not imply recall. Grammar recognition (choose the form) should come before grammar recall (type the form), and a typed grammar form should credit the choose-form skill.

claims.claim: A follow-up with a larger, cross-L1 sample found the same order: recognition came before recall for every component, and the order of acquisition was consistent across L1 backgrounds.
claims.source: González-Fernández, B. (2025). How is vocabulary learnt? An acquisitional sequence of L2 word knowledge. TESOL Quarterly. DOI 10.1002/tesq.3342
claims.numbers: N = 314 EFL learners, L1 Chinese and L1 Spanish
claims.population: EFL learners, L1 Chinese and Spanish
claims.relevance: Suggests the recognition-before-recall implication holds across languages. This matters because Fluenough teaches many target languages and has learners with different L1s.

claims.claim: Phonological (aural) and orthographic (written) receptive vocabulary sizes correlated at 0.68. They do not grow in proportion: at the start of learning, aural vocabulary is often larger than written vocabulary, but written vocabulary then grows faster and is larger at intermediate and advanced levels. L1 Arabic learners were slower to build written vocabulary.
claims.source: Milton, J. & Hopkins, N. (2006). Comparing phonological and orthographic vocabulary size: Do vocabulary tests underestimate the knowledge of some learners? Canadian Modern Language Review 63(1), 127-147. DOI 10.1353/cml.2006.0048
claims.numbers: r = 0.68 between AuralLex and X-Lex (yes/no tests); N = 126 (38 L1 Arabic, 88 L1 Greek)
claims.population: L1 Greek and L1 Arabic learners of English, beginner to advanced
claims.relevance: This is the source of the app's .68 weight. It is a person-level correlation of overall vocabulary size, not a word-level transfer rate. It measures receptive aural vs receptive written recognition only, which is closest to Hear vs Recognition in the app and says nothing about Say or Write. The aural-written gap also depends on proficiency and script (Arabic speakers were slower on written forms), so for learners of Indic scripts, Hear should lead Recognition early on rather than be tied to it symmetrically.

claims.claim: Aural vocabulary size (AuralLex) predicted IELTS listening better than written vocabulary size (X-Lex), and AuralLex also correlated with IELTS speaking. In this smaller sample, aural and written size correlated only at about .46.
claims.source: Milton, J., Wade, J. & Hopkins, N. (2010). Aural word recognition and oral competence in English as a foreign language. In Chacón-Beltrán et al. (eds.), Insights into Non-native Vocabulary Teaching and Learning, Multilingual Matters, 83-98. DOI 10.21832/9781847692900-007
claims.numbers: AuralLex with IELTS listening r = .67; X-Lex with IELTS listening r = .48; AuralLex with IELTS speaking r = .71; AuralLex with X-Lex r = .46 (per a secondary review)
claims.population: EFL learners (small sample, details not retrieved)
claims.relevance: Aural word knowledge goes with oral skills (listening and speaking) more closely than written knowledge does. This argues for a larger cross-weight between Hear and Say than between Hear and Write, and shows that the aural-written link (.46 to .68) varies a lot from study to study.

claims.claim: Studies that measured receptive written and aural vocabulary directly report correlations from moderate to very high. No meta-analysis pooling aural-written vocabulary correlations was found; the expected 'Uchihara et al. ~2024' meta-analysis of aural vs written vocabulary could not be located.
claims.source: Masrai, A. (2019/2020). Exploring the impact of individual differences in aural vocabulary knowledge, written vocabulary knowledge and working memory capacity on explaining L2 learners' listening comprehension (journal details not verified). And: Exploring the relationships between various dimensions of receptive vocabulary knowledge and L2 listening and reading comprehension (2021), Language Testing in Asia 11, DOI 10.1186/s40468-021-00131-8
claims.numbers: Masrai: written-aural receptive r = .58 (p < .001). Language Testing in Asia 2021: orthographic-aural r = .88 (SEM latent correlation, N = 234 Chinese EFL students).
claims.population: Saudi (Masrai) and Chinese university EFL learners
claims.relevance: Puts .68 in context: reported values run from .46 to .88, and latent (error-corrected) correlations are higher. Treat .68 as a midpoint, not a settled constant.

claims.claim: Meta-analysis: overall vocabulary knowledge correlates about .57 with L2 reading and .56 with L2 listening. All three form-meaning mastery levels (meaning recognition, meaning recall, form recall) correlate moderately to highly with both. Meaning recall correlates most strongly with reading, and form recall most strongly with listening. Written vocabulary measures predict reading better; aural measures predict listening better.
claims.source: Zhang, S. & Zhang, X. (2022; online 2020). The relationship between vocabulary knowledge and L2 reading/listening comprehension: A meta-analysis. Language Teaching Research 26(4), 696-725. DOI 10.1177/1362168820913998
claims.numbers: 276 effect sizes, more than 100 studies, about 21,000 learners. r = .57 with reading, r = .56 with listening; disattenuated range .56-.67 (31%-45% of variance). Per-mode coefficients not retrieved; for reading, meaning recall > form recall > meaning recognition.
claims.population: L2 learners across many L1s and L2s (mostly EFL)
claims.relevance: Reading-passage questions are evidence about written-meaning skills (Recognition, especially recall). Listening content is evidence about Hear. The skill whose test matches the modality is the best predictor, which supports weighting answers by modality match rather than with one shared weight.

claims.claim: Meaning recall and meaning recognition behave as separate constructs. In regression on reading proficiency, meaning recall added significant unique variance beyond recognition, but recognition added nothing beyond recall.
claims.source: Stewart, J., Gyllstad, H., Nicklin, C. & McLean, S. (2024). Establishing meaning recall and meaning recognition vocabulary knowledge as distinct psychometric constructs in relation to reading proficiency. Language Testing 41(1), 89-108. DOI 10.1177/02655322231162853
claims.numbers: Factor-fit and correlation values not retrieved
claims.population: Japanese university EFL learners (TOEIC-based sample, not verified)
claims.relevance: Gives a direction: the recall result (self-rated reveal, typed meaning) contains the recognition information but not the reverse. A correct multiple-choice answer (chooseMeaning, matchPairs) should count for less, and should move the recall estimate less, than a correct recall.

claims.claim: For aural (phonological) vocabulary, meaning recognition and meaning recall load on one 'declarative' factor. A timed lexicosemantic judgment task (judging whether a heard word is used correctly in a sentence) loads on a separate 'automatized' factor and best predicts real listening comprehension (TOEIC).
claims.source: Uchihara, T., Saito, K., Kurokawa, S., Takizawa, K. & Suzukida, Y. (2025). Declarative and automatized phonological vocabulary knowledge: Recognition, recall, lexicosemantic judgment, and listening-focused employability of second language words. Language Learning 75(2), 458-492. DOI 10.1111/lang.12668
claims.numbers: N = 114 L1 Japanese learners of English; SEM with two latent factors (exact loadings not retrieved; the paper has a 2026 correction)
claims.relevance: Within Hear, choosing a heard word's meaning and typing it are close to interchangeable (one factor), so they can share one schedule. Fast, in-context listening (heard words inside sentences or passages) is a further level that isolated-word recognition does not imply. This is probably the closest Uchihara work to what the brief asked for; it is not a meta-analysis.

claims.claim: Productive phonological vocabulary (partial dictation) correlated more strongly with listening than with reading. Productive written vocabulary correlated about equally with both.
claims.source: Cheng, J. & Matthews, J. (2018). The relationship between three measures of L2 vocabulary knowledge and L2 listening and reading. Language Testing 35(1), 3-25. DOI 10.1177/0265532216676851
claims.numbers: N = 250 EFL students. Productive phonological with listening r = .71, with reading r = .46. Productive orthographic with listening r = .55, with reading r = .57 (from citing studies; secondary sources disagree slightly on the reading figure).
claims.relevance: Dictation (hear the word, type it) is a productive phonological task and is the best vocabulary predictor of listening. It is evidence for Hear and for spelling (Write type), so one dictation answer could update both.

claims.claim: Receptive vocabulary (L2 to L1 translation) was larger than productive vocabulary (L1 to L2 translation). With full-knowledge scoring, the gap widened as word frequency fell. With partial-knowledge scoring, there was little difference. Learners with larger receptive vocabularies also knew more of those words productively.
claims.source: Webb, S. (2008). Receptive and productive vocabulary sizes of L2 learners. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 30(1), 79-95. DOI 10.1017/S0272263108080042
claims.numbers: N = 83 L1 Japanese second-year EFL university students; bands 701-1,900, 1,901-3,400, 3,401-6,600. A secondary source gives the productive-to-receptive ratio as 77% (not verified); reviews give 50-80% across studies.
claims.relevance: Knowing a word receptively predicts productive knowledge only partly (roughly 50-80%), and less for rarer words. Credit from Recognition to Write or Say should be smaller for low-frequency words. Partial credit (near-misses in typed or spoken answers) closes much of the gap.

claims.claim: Passive (receptive) vocabulary was always significantly larger than controlled active and free active vocabulary. The gap was smaller for foreign-language learners in Israel than for second-language learners in Canada, and it narrowed only after about two years of living in the L2 setting. A companion study found that passive and controlled active sizes correlated well, but free active (spontaneous use in writing) did not correlate with either.
claims.source: Laufer, B. & Paribakht, T. S. (1998). The relationship between passive and active vocabularies: Effects of language learning context. Language Learning 48(3), 365-391. DOI 10.1111/0023-8333.00046. Companion: Laufer, B. (1998). The development of passive and active vocabulary in a second language: Same or different? Applied Linguistics 19(2), 255-271
claims.numbers: N = 79 (Israel) and N = 103 (Canada) adult EFL/ESL learners. Correlation coefficients not retrieved.
claims.population: Adult learners of English, L1 Hebrew/Arabic (Israel) and mixed L1 (Canada)
claims.relevance: Controlled production (typing a word when prompted) follows receptive knowledge closely. Free production does not. Inside the app, all production is prompted, so a moderate cross-weight from Recognition to Write is defensible. It should not be taken to mean free speaking ability.

claims.claim: Direction of learning matters. Productive learning of word pairs gave larger gains in orthography (both receptive and productive) and in productive knowledge of meaning, syntax and grammatical functions. Receptive learning was better only for receptive knowledge of meaning. Webb concludes that if only one method is used, productive learning may be more effective.
claims.source: Webb, S. (2009). The effects of receptive and productive learning of word pairs on vocabulary knowledge. RELC Journal 40(3), 360-376. DOI 10.1177/0033688209343854
claims.numbers: 10 test formats per word across 5 aspects; scores and effect sizes not retrieved
claims.relevance: Direct evidence of asymmetric transfer between practice directions. Practicing production (chooseWord, typing, Say) transfers to receptive skills. Practicing reception transfers to production less. So the transfer weight from Write/Say to Recognition should be larger than the weight from Recognition to Write/Say.

claims.claim: When time on task was equal, a productive task (writing sentences with target words) produced more receptive and more productive knowledge than a receptive task (reading glossed sentences).
claims.source: Webb, S. (2005). Receptive and productive vocabulary learning: The effects of reading and writing on word knowledge. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 27(1), 33-52. DOI 10.1017/S0272263105050023
claims.numbers: Effect sizes not retrieved
claims.relevance: Supports the same direction as Webb 2009: success at production is good evidence of receptive knowledge as well.

claims.claim: Across a review of word-list learning experiments, receptive learning is easier and gives higher receptive scores. Scores are highest when the direction of learning matches the direction of testing. Productive learning yields a considerable amount of receptive knowledge, while receptive learning yields less productive knowledge.
claims.source: Mondria, J.-A. & Wiersma, B. (2004). Receptive, productive, and receptive + productive L2 vocabulary learning: What difference does it make? In Bogaards & Laufer (eds.), Vocabulary in a Second Language, John Benjamins, 79-100. DOI 10.1075/lllt.10.08mon
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.population: Dutch secondary-school learners of French (from memory of the chapter; not verified here)
claims.relevance: Another source for asymmetric transfer: productive success should credit receptive skills strongly, receptive success should credit productive skills weakly. Because of the direction-matching effect, each skill still needs its own schedule; cross-skill credit should be partial, not full.

claims.claim: For idioms learned as paired associates, direction of learning affected performance, with an especially large effect on the productive test that persisted at a 3-week delayed test. Productive learners did better on productive tests, and receptive learners did better on receptive tests.
claims.source: Steinel, M. P., Hulstijn, J. H. & Steinel, W. (2007). Second language idiom learning in a paired-associate paradigm: Effects of direction of learning, direction of testing, idiom imageability, and idiom transparency. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 29(3), 449-484. DOI 10.1017/S0272263107070271
claims.numbers: 20 English idioms; Dutch university students; 80 raters in the norming study; effect sizes not retrieved
claims.relevance: Transfer between directions is incomplete even for multiword units. Separate Recognition and Write schedules are justified; cross-skill updates should be partial.

claims.claim: Size and depth relate in a way that depends on frequency and learner level. For high-frequency words and learners with small vocabularies, there is often little difference between size and depth measures. For rarer words and larger vocabularies, depth falls behind size. Some depth aspects (for example derivatives) correlate with size less strongly than others, and depth usually adds explanatory power beyond size.
claims.source: Schmitt, N. (2014). Size and depth of vocabulary knowledge: What the research shows. Language Learning 64(4), 913-951. DOI 10.1111/lang.12077
claims.numbers: The abstract gives no single coefficient
claims.relevance: Cross-skill implication should be stronger for frequent words and beginners, and weaker for rare words and advanced learners. The transfer weight could be made to depend on word frequency or difficulty instead of being a constant.

gaps: WebFetch and direct access to publisher pages (Wiley, OUP, SAGE, ERIC, White Rose, Project MUSE) were blocked in this environment, so most numbers come from abstracts and citing studies returned by WebSearch. Before hard-coding any number, check it against the original paper.

No 'Uchihara et al. ~2024' meta-analysis of aural vs written vocabulary was found. Uchihara's related work is the 2025 Language Learning study (declarative vs automatized phonological knowledge) and Uchihara & Clenton 2020 (vocabulary size and speaking, LTR, DOI 10.1177/1362168818799371, not examined). No pooled aural-written correlation exists in what was found; individual studies range from r = .46 to .88.
Milton (2009), Measuring Second Language Vocabulary Acquisition (Multilingual Matters), was not retrieved; its aural/written figures are unverified.

González-Fernández & Schmitt 2020: the component correlation coefficients and the implicational-scaling reproducibility and scalability coefficients were not retrieved. Laufer & Goldstein 2004: scale coefficients not retrieved, and the .65 correlation with achievement comes only from a secondary summary.

No study found gives word-level transfer probabilities (P(skill B correct | skill A correct on the same word)), which is what an FSRS/Elo cross-update actually needs. The correlations above are person-level vocabulary-size correlations. That makes them an upper bound on how much one answer about one word should move another skill. Logging the app's own same-word, cross-skill outcomes would allow this to be fitted directly.

No research found on transfer to speaking graded by speech recognition (Say) from other skills, beyond Milton et al. 2010 (AuralLex with IELTS speaking r = .71). Nothing specific was found on transfer for script dictation, transliteration typing, or Indic-script learners.
Mondria & Wiersma 2004 population details are from memory, not verified.

checked.claim: Laufer & Goldstein (2004): four strength levels form a difficulty hierarchy (active recall hardest, then passive recall, active recognition, passive recognition easiest); the abstract says it held at every frequency level; the levels are framed as an implicational scale.
checked.source: Laufer, B. & Goldstein, Z. (2004). Testing vocabulary knowledge: Size, strength, and computer adaptiveness. Language Learning 54(3), 399-436. DOI 10.1111/j.0023-8333.2004.00260.x
checked.correction: The source exists as cited (Language Learning 54(3), 399-436; N = 435 learners of English). Several secondary sources (reviews, and the CATSS test site, which calls the levels an implicational scale) give the hierarchy in this order: passive recognition easiest, then active recognition, then passive recall, with active recall hardest. I could not open the abstract, because the Wiley, Crossref and OpenAlex pages were all unreachable. So the claim that 'the abstract says the hierarchy held at every frequency level' is unverified. The .65 correlation with achievement and the 'mostly L1 Hebrew' description come only from an auto-generated FAQ on the academia.edu page; treat both as unverified. Lower confidence to Medium for the order of the hierarchy and Low for the frequency-level and implicational-scale details. Do not confuse this paper with Laufer, Elder, Hill & Congdon (2004), Language Testing, which is a separate paper about the same test.

checked.claim: González-Fernández & Schmitt (2020): across four components (form-meaning, derivatives, multiple meanings, collocations), recognition of every component came before recall of any component; implicational scaling found a consistent order; the components were closely related.
checked.source: González-Fernández, B. & Schmitt, N. (2020; online Jan 2019). Applied Linguistics 41(4), 481-505. DOI 10.1093/applin/amy057
checked.correction: The source exists, and the DOI amy057 is correct; amy052 is wrong. N = 144 Spanish learners of English. The abstract, as summarised in search results, says the components were strongly intercorrelated. Implicational scaling showed a consistent order, with recognition knowledge emerging before recall knowledge for each component. SEM showed that all components contribute to the overall construct, but that recognition and recall mastery of a given component should be treated as separate constructs. The wording 'recognition of every component came before recall of ANY component' is stronger than what I could verify. The source says recognition comes before recall within each component. The year is often cited as 2019 because of the online-first date. Correlation values were not retrieved.

checked.claim: González-Fernández (2025): with a larger cross-L1 sample, recognition came before recall for every component, and the order was consistent across L1 backgrounds.
checked.source: González-Fernández, B. (2025; online July 2024). How is vocabulary learnt? An acquisitional sequence of L2 word knowledge. TESOL Quarterly 59(2), 755-784. DOI 10.1002/tesq.3342
checked.correction: Confirmed from the abstract text shown on Wiley and ERIC. N = 314 EFL learners with L1 Chinese and L1 Spanish. Implicational and Mokken scaling found a reliable hierarchy in which recognition came before recall across all components. The scale held for both L1 groups, analysed separately and together, at 75% and 80% accuracy thresholds. Missing details: volume, issue and pages (59(2), 755-784). Note that only written form and meaning tests were used, so this says nothing about aural or spoken skills. It is open access (White Rose repository).

checked.claim: Milton & Hopkins (2006): phonological and orthographic receptive vocabulary sizes correlated at 0.68; they do not grow in proportion (aural larger at the start, written grows faster and is larger at intermediate and advanced levels); L1 Arabic learners were slower to build written vocabulary.
checked.source: Milton, J. & Hopkins, N. (2006). Canadian Modern Language Review 63(1), 127-147. DOI 10.1353/cml.2006.0048
checked.correction: The citation is correct. Several citing sources confirm r = 0.68 between the AuralLex (A-Lex) and X-Lex yes/no tests, with samples of 38 Arabic-speaking and 88 Greek-speaking learners. A secondary summary supports 'Arabic speakers rather slower to develop the orthographic side'. Another secondary summary adds that the two groups scored similarly on X-Lex, but the Arabic group scored significantly higher on AuralLex (p < .01). I could NOT verify the growth pattern ('written grows faster and is larger at intermediate/advanced') from any text I could reach. Downgrade confidence from High to Medium: the abstract and full text were not reachable. The researcher's point that this is a person-level correlation from receptive yes/no tests is correct, and later authors make the same criticism of the yes/no format.

checked.claim: Milton, Wade & Hopkins (2010): AuralLex predicted IELTS listening better than X-Lex; AuralLex correlated with IELTS speaking; aural-written size correlated at about .46.
checked.source: Milton, J., Wade, J. & Hopkins, N. (2010). Aural word recognition and oral competence in English as a foreign language. Multilingual Matters, 83-98. DOI 10.21832/9781847692900-007
checked.correction: The book title is wrong. The chapter is in Chacón-Beltrán, Abello-Contesse & Torreblanca-López (eds.), *Further* Insights into Non-native Vocabulary Teaching and Learning (2010), pp. 83-98. 'Insights into...' is the earlier 2006 volume. All figures come from citing papers, not the chapter itself. AuralLex: IELTS listening r = .67 and speaking r = .71; reading .22 and writing .44. X-Lex: listening .48 and speaking .35; reading .70 and writing .76. One secondary source, which is somewhat garbled, gives aural-written r = 0.46 with N = 30 (10 Arabic, 10 Chinese, 10 Japanese/European learners). Treat .46 as Low confidence. The sample is very small (about 30).

checked.claim: Masrai: written-aural receptive r = .58; Language Testing in Asia 2021: orthographic-aural r = .88 (SEM latent, N = 234 Chinese EFL); no meta-analysis pooling aural-written correlations was found.
checked.source: Masrai, A. (2020; online 2019). Applied Linguistics Review 11(3), 423-447. DOI 10.1515/applirev-2018-0106. Ha, H. T. (2021). Language Testing in Asia 11, article 20. DOI 10.1186/s40468-021-00131-8
checked.correction: There are two errors. (1) The Language Testing in Asia 2021 paper is by Hung Tan Ha, not Masrai. Its sample was 234 tertiary-level VIETNAMESE EFL learners, not Chinese. It used the UVLT, a Vietnamese version of the LVLT, and IELTS listening and academic reading. It reports orthographic-aural r = .88 and calls the two 'of equal significance' to listening and reading. I could not confirm whether .88 is a latent SEM correlation or an observed one. (2) The Masrai paper is in Applied Linguistics Review 11(3), 423-447 (2020; online 2019), with N = 130 non-native speakers of English. In it, aural vocabulary was the strongest predictor of listening, then working memory, and written vocabulary added only marginally. I could not find the r = .58 figure in any accessible text, so it is unsupported. I also found no meta-analysis pooling aural-written vocabulary correlations. Zhang & Zhang (2022) treats modality only as a moderator of the vocabulary-comprehension correlation.

checked.claim: Zhang & Zhang meta-analysis: vocabulary correlates about .57 with L2 reading and .56 with listening; all three mastery levels correlate moderately to highly; meaning recall correlates most with reading and form recall most with listening; written measures predict reading better and aural measures predict listening better.
checked.source: Zhang, S. & Zhang, X. (2022; online 31 Mar 2020). Language Teaching Research 26(4), 696-725. DOI 10.1177/1362168820913998
checked.correction: Confirmed from abstract text: r = .57 with reading and .56 with listening (p < .01); true correlation likely .56-.67 (31%-45% of variance); more than 100 studies and 276 effect sizes. Meaning recall correlated most strongly with reading and form recall most strongly with listening. Orthographic measures correlated more strongly with reading than auditory measures did, and auditory measures were better predictors of listening. Caveat: Stewart et al. (2021, VLI 10(2)) note that form recall's lead over meaning recall for listening was not statistically significant.

checked.claim: Stewart et al. (2024): meaning recall and meaning recognition are separate constructs; meaning recall added unique variance in reading beyond recognition, but recognition added nothing beyond recall.
checked.source: Stewart, J., Gyllstad, H., Nicklin, C. & McLean, S. (2024). Language Testing 41(1), 89-108. DOI 10.1177/02655322231162853
checked.correction: Confirmed from the abstract. A two-factor model fit better than one factor, but the authors say discriminant validity between the factors is questionable, so the 'separate constructs' framing should be hedged. Recognition made no significant contribution beyond recall, while recall did contribute beyond recognition. The authors conclude that recognition does not tap unique aspects of vocabulary knowledge. The population ('Japanese university EFL, TOEIC-based') was not verified. Effect sizes were not retrieved, although the paper is open access.

checked.claim: Uchihara et al. (2025): for aural vocabulary, meaning recognition and recall form one declarative factor; a timed lexicosemantic judgment task loads on a separate automatized factor and best predicts TOEIC listening.
checked.source: Uchihara, T., Saito, K., Kurokawa, S., Takizawa, K. & Suzukida, Y. (2025; online Aug 2024). Language Learning 75(2), 458-492. DOI 10.1111/lang.12668
checked.correction: Confirmed from abstract text. N = 114 Japanese learners of English took TOEIC Listening plus aural meaning recognition, meaning recall and the LJT. The LJT best predicted access to target words in real listening, measured by TOEIC. SEM showed the LJT was distinct from both recognition and recall. The detail that recognition and recall grouped on one factor comes from a later paper by the same group (Saito et al.) describing this study. Loadings were not retrieved. A follow-up study by the same group reports LJT-TOEIC r = .64 against about .45 for recognition; that figure is from the follow-up, not this paper.

checked.claim: Cheng & Matthews (2018): productive phonological vocabulary correlated more with listening (.71) than reading (.46); productive written vocabulary correlated about equally with both (.55 listening, .57 reading).
checked.source: Cheng, J. & Matthews, J. (2018). Language Testing 35(1), 3-25. DOI 10.1177/0265532216676851
checked.correction: Confirmed. The ERIC abstract gives N = 250 tertiary-level Chinese EFL learners. Productive phonological knowledge correlated most strongly with listening (r = .71) and explained 51% of the variance in listening. Productive orthographic knowledge correlated most strongly with reading (r = .57) and explained 33% of the variance in reading. The other figures come from Ha (2021): productive phonological with reading .46, productive orthographic with listening .55. I could not confirm from accessible text that the phonological test was a 'partial dictation' format.

checked.claim: Webb (2008): receptive (L2 to L1) vocabulary larger than productive; with full-knowledge scoring the gap widened as frequency fell; with partial scoring there was little difference; larger receptive vocabularies go with more productive knowledge of those words.
checked.source: Webb, S. (2008). Studies in Second Language Acquisition 30(1), 79-95. DOI 10.1017/S0272263108080042
checked.correction: Confirmed from the ERIC abstract and summaries. N = 83 L1 Japanese second-year EFL university students. Frequency bands were 701-1,900, 1,901-3,400 and 3,401-6,600. The ratio claim needs correcting. An unofficial copy of the paper reports productive-to-receptive ratios of roughly 91-95% under sensitive (partial) scoring and 65-88% under strict scoring. Lee (2025) cites a single 77%. The '50-80%' figure in the relevance note comes from reviews of other studies, not from Webb 2008.

checked.claim: Laufer & Paribakht (1998): passive vocabulary always larger than controlled and free active; gap smaller in FL Israel than L2 Canada; narrowed only after about 2 years of residence. Companion Laufer (1998): passive and controlled active correlated well, free active did not correlate with either.
checked.source: Laufer, B. & Paribakht, T. S. (1998). Language Learning 48(3), 365-391. DOI 10.1111/0023-8333.00046. Laufer, B. (1998). Applied Linguistics 19(2), 255-271
checked.correction: Both are confirmed from abstract text. Laufer & Paribakht: N = 79 adults in Israel and 103 in Canada. Passive vocabulary was always significantly larger, and the passive-active gap was smaller in the FL context than the L2 context. Residence in the L2 context began to help only after about 2 years. Knowledge of French helped Canadian learners at early stages. Laufer (1998): N = 48 Israeli high-school ESL students over one year. Passive and controlled active correlated well, while free active did not correlate with either. Some reference lists wrongly give vol. 12; the correct volume is 19. The L1s (Hebrew/Arabic) were not verified, and correlation coefficients were not retrieved.

checked.claim: Webb (2009): productive learning of word pairs gave larger gains in orthography (receptive and productive) and productive meaning, syntax and grammatical functions; receptive learning better only for receptive meaning; if only one method, productive may be more effective.
checked.correction: Confirmed from abstract text, which matches nearly verbatim. Population: N = 84 Japanese EFL students. Five aspects of word knowledge were tested in 10 ways. Effect sizes were not retrieved.

checked.claim: Webb (2005): with equal time on task, a productive task (writing sentences) produced more receptive and productive knowledge than a receptive task (reading glossed sentences).
checked.source: Webb, S. (2005). Studies in Second Language Acquisition 27(1), 33-52. DOI 10.1017/S0272263105050023
checked.correction: This claim reverses the finding. In Experiment 1, with EQUAL time on both tasks, the READING (receptive) task was superior. The writing task was more effective only in Experiment 2, where time depended on how long each task took to complete, and writing needed more time. Webb argues for productive tasks only if Experiment 2 represents authentic learning. The study does not support 'production beats reception at equal time'.

checked.claim: Mondria & Wiersma (2004): a review of word-list learning experiments finds receptive learning easier with higher receptive scores; scores highest when learning direction matches test direction; productive learning yields considerable receptive knowledge, receptive learning yields less productive knowledge.
checked.source: Mondria, J.-A. & Wiersma, B. (2004). In Bogaards & Laufer (eds.), Vocabulary in a Second Language, John Benjamins, 79-100. DOI 10.1075/lllt.10.08mon
checked.correction: The chapter exists as cited, and a Dutch version is in Levende Talen Tijdschrift 5(3), 29-37. It reports the authors' own experiment, not a review of experiments. Only secondary sources were available. One review says the authors conclude that receptive learning is easier and gives higher receptive scores, and that productive learning yields a considerable amount of receptive knowledge while the reverse effect is less strong. Other sources cite the chapter for a direction-matching effect. The participants were not verified: the Dutch secondary-school context is implied by the motivation (Dutch exams), but the target language and N were not confirmed. Medium confidence for the conclusions, Low for the population.

checked.claim: Steinel, Hulstijn & Steinel (2007): for idioms learned as paired associates, direction of learning affected performance, with an especially large effect on the productive test that persisted at a 3-week delayed test; productive learners did better on productive tests, receptive learners on receptive tests.
checked.source: Steinel, M. P., Hulstijn, J. H. & Steinel, W. (2007). Studies in Second Language Acquisition 29(3), 449-484. DOI 10.1017/S0272263107070271
checked.correction: The citation is correct; the ResearchGate title is truncated, and the full title includes 'direction of learning'. What I could verify: Dutch university students learned English idioms as L1-L2 or L2-L1 pairs, and direction of learning affected both receptive and productive performance. Imageability predicted performance, and receptive learning was especially weak for low-imageability idioms. Transparency affected only recognition. The n = 80 is described as an independent follow-up sample that qualified the findings, not as 80 norming raters. I could NOT verify the 'especially large effect on the productive test' or the '3-week delayed test', so treat both as unsupported until the abstract is read.

checked.claim: Schmitt (2014): size-depth relation depends on frequency and learner level; little difference for high-frequency words and small vocabularies; depth lags size for rarer words and larger vocabularies; derivatives correlate less with size; depth usually adds explanatory power beyond size.
checked.source: Schmitt, N. (2014). Size and depth of vocabulary knowledge: What the research shows. Language Learning 64(4), 913-951. DOI 10.1111/lang.12077
checked.correction: Confirmed from abstract text: each point matches. It is a critical synthesis, not new data, and gives no single coefficient. An author version is in the Nottingham repository. Process note for all rows: WebFetch and direct API access (Wiley, Crossref, OpenAlex, ERIC pages) failed in this environment, so every check relied on search-result abstract text. The web-search budget ran out before a final Steinel check.

claims.claim: Laufer and Goldstein treat word-meaning knowledge as four 'strength' modalities, ordered by difficulty from easiest to hardest: passive recognition (see L2 word, pick meaning), active recognition (see meaning, pick L2 word), passive recall (see L2 word, supply meaning), active recall (see meaning, supply L2 word). The hierarchy held at every word-frequency level. Passive recall was the best predictor of classroom language performance.
claims.source: Laufer, B. & Goldstein, Z. (2004). Testing vocabulary knowledge: Size, strength, and computer adaptiveness. Language Learning 54(3), 399-436.
claims.population: 435 learners of English as an L2 (Israeli high school and university students), Hebrew-English bilingual computerized test
claims.numbers: N=435. Order: passive recognition < active recognition < passive recall < active recall. One third-party summary gives passive recall's correlation with classroom performance as about .65; not checked against the paper.
claims.relevance: This is the backbone mapping. chooseMeaning = meaning recognition. chooseWord = form recognition. Self-rated reveal and hear-and-type-meaning = meaning recall. Typing the word from its meaning (and speak) = form recall. Because the scale is implicational, a correct answer at a harder level implies the easier levels, but an easier success says little about harder ones. Cross-skill updates should therefore be asymmetric: a correct form recall should move recognition strongly, while a correct recognition should move recall only weakly. A failed recognition should move recall down strongly. Confidence is Medium because I could not open the abstract myself; I read it through search snippets of ResearchGate and Semantic Scholar listings.

claims.claim: Across four word-knowledge components (form-meaning link, derivatives, multiple meanings, collocations), all components were strongly intercorrelated. Implicational scaling showed a consistent acquisition order, with recognition mastered before recall for every component.
claims.source: González-Fernández, B. & Schmitt, N. (2020). Word knowledge: Exploring the relationships and order of acquisition of vocabulary knowledge components. Applied Linguistics 41(4), 481-505.
claims.numbers: N=144. 'Strongly intercorrelated' (I did not retrieve the exact r values). Recognition precedes recall for all four components.
claims.relevance: This supports one shared latent ability with ordered thresholds rather than independent skills. A single global cross-skill weight is too coarse: recognition-to-recall implication runs one way. Collocation and form-meaning knowledge correlate, so cloze answers carry some information about the word's form-meaning link. The DOI was recalled from memory; the search confirmed only the journal, volume and pages.

claims.claim: Meaning recall and meaning recognition were examined as possibly psychometrically distinct constructs, using confirmatory factor analysis and hierarchical regression on L2 reading proficiency. A citing paper reports the conclusion that meaning-recall tests predict reading better than multiple-choice meaning-recognition tests.
claims.source: Stewart, J., Gyllstad, H., Nicklin, C. & McLean, S. (2024; online 2023). Establishing meaning recall and meaning recognition vocabulary knowledge as distinct psychometric constructs in relation to reading proficiency. Language Testing 41(1), 89-108.
claims.population: Japanese university EFL learners (assumed from the authors' usual samples; not confirmed)
claims.numbers: I did not retrieve the factor loadings or the incremental R².
claims.relevance: chooseMeaning (recognition) and recall formats (self-rated reveal, hear-and-type) should not be treated as the same evidence. Recall answers should carry more weight for the Recognition skill's ability estimate, and MC answers less.

claims.claim: Multiple-choice meaning-recognition tests (Vocabulary Size Test variants) correlate highly with meaning recall, at r = .88 to .91 for three variants and r = .77 for the bilingual variant with an 'I don't know' option. The authors recommend measuring meaning recall, or adjusting raw MC scores, because MC overestimates.
claims.source: Stoeckel, T. et al. (2019), comparing four VST variants against a meaning-recall criterion (reported through a secondary summary; I did not confirm the exact title or venue)
claims.population: Japanese university EFL learners (per secondary summary)
claims.numbers: r = .88-.91 (three variants); r = .77 (bilingual with 'I don't know' option)
claims.relevance: Use this to weight transfer from chooseMeaning to meaning recall: a correct 4-option MC answer is noisy evidence of recall because of guessing (25% chance) and elimination. Discount MC successes before propagating them. The URL is the review where I found this claim (Stoeckel, McLean & Nation 2021, SSLA), not the 2019 paper itself.

claims.claim: A meaning-recognition test and a parallel meaning-recall test correlated almost identically with reading comprehension, with no significant difference between them.
claims.source: Laufer, B. & Aviad-Levitzky, T. (2017). What type of vocabulary knowledge predicts reading comprehension: Word meaning recall or word meaning recognition? Modern Language Journal 101(4).
claims.numbers: r = .91 and .92 with reading
claims.relevance: At the level of the learner's ability, recognition and recall share most of their variance (correlation about .9), so updating the language-level ability across these formats is justified. Per-word implication is weaker, as the claims above show. The venue was recalled from memory; the numbers come from a secondary summary.

claims.claim: The Vocabulary Levels Test, in its 2017 update, uses a matching format (three definitions matched to words from a set of six) to measure recognition of form-meaning connections at the 1000-5000 frequency levels. It was validated with Rasch analysis under Messick's framework.
claims.source: Webb, S., Sasao, Y. & Ballance, O. (2017). The updated Vocabulary Levels Test: Developing and validating two new forms of the VLT. ITL - International Journal of Applied Linguistics 168(1), 33-69.
claims.population: 1,463 test takers to select items, plus 250 to evaluate the forms; EFL learners from several L1s
claims.relevance: matchPairs measures form-meaning recognition, much like chooseMeaning and chooseWord. In a 4-pair match, the last pair is forced by elimination, so it carries little evidence and should be weighted lower. The 3-from-6 item format comes from memory of the original VLT; search results only confirmed 'recognize the form-meaning connections'.

claims.claim: Kremmel and Schmitt question whether scores on the common item formats (VLT matching, VST multiple choice, form recall, meaning recall) show that learners can actually use the words in the four skills or know deeper aspects such as derivatives and collocations. They report that little is known about how informative each format is about 'lexical employability'.
claims.source: Kremmel, B. & Schmitt, N. (2016). Interpreting vocabulary test scores: What do various item formats tell us about learners' ability to employ words? Language Assessment Quarterly 13(4), 377-392.
claims.numbers: I did not retrieve per-format agreement rates.
claims.relevance: This is a caution: no single format implies use in all skills. Writing transfer weights per format, instead of one global .68, follows the authors' call for format-specific interpretation.

claims.claim: Schmitt, Nation and Kremmel argue that most recently published vocabulary tests lack adequate validation. They call for tests to state their purpose and intended score interpretation precisely, including which kind of knowledge each format measures.
claims.source: Schmitt, N., Nation, P. & Kremmel, B. (2020). Moving the field of vocabulary assessment forward: The need for more rigorous test development and validation. Language Teaching 53(1), 109-120.
claims.relevance: This supports the principle that each question type should be mapped to an explicit knowledge component (meaning recognition, form recall, and so on) instead of a generic 'skill'.

claims.claim: Aural (phonological) and written (orthographic) vocabulary size, each measured with a yes/no checklist (AuralLex and X_Lex), correlated at r = .68. Arabic L1 learners scored similarly to Greek learners on the written test but significantly higher on the aural test, so written tests may underestimate some learners.
claims.source: Milton, J. & Hopkins, N. (2006). Comparing phonological and orthographic vocabulary size: Do vocabulary tests underestimate the knowledge of some learners? Canadian Modern Language Review 63(1), 127-147.
claims.population: 38 Arabic L1 and 88 Greek L1 learners of English
claims.numbers: r = .68. Arabic > Greek on AuralLex, p < .01.
claims.relevance: This is the source of the app's current .68 weight. It is a between-learner correlation of yes/no form-recognition size estimates, not a within-word transfer rate, and it covers only Hear versus written recognition.
