It does not justify using .68 for Say or Write (form recall), and the gap depends on the script (L1 script distance). A later review cautions that yes/no formats limit what can be concluded.

claims.claim: Among Chinese EFL learners, productive phonological vocabulary knowledge correlated most strongly with L2 listening (r = .71), and productive orthographic vocabulary knowledge correlated most strongly with L2 reading (r = .57).
claims.source: Cheng, J. & Matthews, J. (2018). The relationship between three measures of L2 vocabulary knowledge and L2 listening and reading. Language Testing 35(1). (Venue from memory; the title is confirmed in the UNE repository.)
claims.numbers: r = .71 (phonological, with listening); r = .57 (orthographic, with reading)
claims.relevance: Modality-specific knowledge predicts its matching skill best. Hear questions (hearMeaning, hear-and-type) are the best evidence for aural form knowledge; written chooseMeaning is weaker evidence for Hear. This supports separate Hear and Recognition abilities with partial, not full, transfer.

claims.claim: Aural vocabulary knowledge was the strongest predictor of listening comprehension, followed by working memory; written vocabulary knowledge added only marginally.
claims.source: Masrai, A. (2020). Applied Linguistics Review (aural vocabulary, written vocabulary, working memory and listening comprehension).
claims.population: Arabic L1 EFL learners (Saudi Arabia; assumed)
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.relevance: This shows aural and written form knowledge are dissociable. Evidence from written questions should transfer to Hear only partially. The URL is the review that summarises the study, not the study itself.

claims.claim: In paired-associate learning of L2 idioms, learning direction interacted with test direction. Productive learners had a sizable advantage on production tests, and receptive learners outperformed them on recognition tests. The authors say this parallels findings for single L2 words.
claims.source: Steinel, M. P., Hulstijn, J. H. & Steinel, W. (2007). Second language idiom learning in a paired-associate paradigm: Effects of direction of learning, direction of testing, idiom imageability, and idiom transparency. Studies in Second Language Acquisition 29, 449-484.
claims.population: 129 Dutch university students learning 20 English idioms; tested immediately and after 3 weeks
claims.numbers: N=129; 20 idioms. The effect sizes were not retrieved.
claims.relevance: Practising in one direction (chooseMeaning, L2 to meaning) builds that direction best, and transfer to the other direction (chooseWord, typing, speak) is partial. A recognition success should update production schedules much less than a same-direction success.

claims.claim: Webb's thesis experiments, reported in RELC Journal 40(3), found that productive word-pair learning develops productive knowledge more, and receptive learning develops receptive knowledge more. In Webb (2005, SSLA), each word was tested in 10 ways across five aspects (orthography, syntax, association, grammatical functions, meaning and form), and both receptive and productive tasks produced gains in several aspects.
claims.source: Webb, S. (2009). The effects of receptive and productive learning of word pairs on vocabulary knowledge. RELC Journal 40(3), 360ff; Webb, S. (2005). Receptive and productive vocabulary learning: The effects of reading and writing on word knowledge. SSLA 27, 33-52.
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.relevance: One kind of practice yields knowledge in several components, but most strongly in the component it exercises (transfer-appropriate). This supports a primary-plus-secondary mapping for each question. The 2009 result comes from the thesis summary, and I am inferring that the article reports the same experiments. The DOI for the 2005 paper is from memory.

claims.claim: Transfer-appropriate processing: semantic encoding beat rhyme encoding on a standard recognition test, but rhyme encoding beat semantic encoding on a rhyme-recognition test. How well memory performs depends on the match between processing at study and at test, not on depth alone.
claims.source: Morris, C. D., Bransford, J. D. & Franks, J. J. (1977). Levels of processing versus transfer appropriate processing. Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 16, 519-533.
claims.numbers: I did not retrieve the exact proportions.
claims.relevance: This is the theoretical basis for treating each question as strongest evidence for the skill whose processing it shares (sound-based questions for Hear, meaning-to-form questions for Say and Write), with weaker evidence for the others. Meaning-only practice may not build phonological form, which supports a low transfer from Recognition to Say. The DOI was recalled from memory.

claims.claim: Retrieval practice transfers to different final tests with an overall mean of about d = 0.40. Without response congruency between the practice and final test, the effect is about d = 0.28; with congruency (overlapping answers), it is about d = 0.58. Elaborated retrieval practice adds about d = 0.23.
claims.source: Pan, S. C. & Rickard, T. C. (2018). Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis. Psychological Bulletin 144(7), 710-756.
claims.population: Meta-analysis of 192 transfer effect sizes, mostly adult L1 learners across many materials
claims.numbers: d ≈ 0.40 overall; d = 0.28 with no response congruency; d = 0.58 with congruency; +0.23 for elaborated feedback
claims.relevance: This gives rough magnitudes: practising the same answer in another format (for example, chooseWord then type the word, both producing the L2 form) transfers about twice as well as practice with a different answer (chooseMeaning, whose answer is the meaning, then speak, whose answer is the form). It supports response-overlap-based cross-skill weights.

claims.claim: Multiple-choice and short-answer initial tests differ in their benefit to retention. Without feedback, an MC test helped more than a short-answer test, because short-answer accuracy was low. With corrective feedback, a short-answer test gave the best final performance, consistent with more effortful retrieval producing more learning.
claims.source: Kang, S. H. K., McDermott, K. B. & Roediger, H. L. (2007). Test format and corrective feedback modify the effect of testing on long-term retention. European Journal of Cognitive Psychology 19(4-5), 528-558.
claims.population: US undergraduates learning facts from journal papers; final test after 3 days
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.relevance: Recall formats (type the word, hear-and-type, speak) are stronger learning events and stronger evidence than recognition formats, so a successful recall should earn a larger FSRS stability gain and Elo move than a recognition success.

claims.claim: Rational-deletion cloze scores were significantly predicted by vocabulary and grammar knowledge. A think-aloud study found that proficient readers used lexical and grammatical knowledge to fill gaps. A factor analysis found that grammar and reading, but not nonverbal closure or reasoning, indicated cloze performance.
claims.source: Rational Cloze Test: A Valid Measure of Vocabulary? Veridian E-Journal (Thai EFL, 2015); McKamey, T. (2006). Getting closure on cloze: A validation study of the 'rational deletion' method. Second Language Studies (University of Hawai'i).
claims.population: 104 Thai EFL students (2015 study); 48 learners (McKamey 2006); 16 proficient readers (2022 think-aloud)
claims.numbers: N=104, 48, 16. Vocabulary and grammar were significant predictors (coefficients not retrieved).
claims.relevance: Cloze (choose or type the missing word) judges Write form knowledge (form recognition if chosen, form recall if typed) in context, plus grammar and collocation. A cloze success should update the word's Write schedule as primary and the related grammar ability as secondary. A failure is ambiguous between vocabulary and grammar. The 2015 study's author is not given here, and these are not top-tier sources.

claims.claim: Dictation was argued to tap general language processing ('analysis by synthesis') and to sample structural and lexical items in context, not just sound-to-letter copying. In a university placement battery, dictation correlated with the total score better than any of the other four subtests, and correlated highly with cloze.
claims.source: Oller, J. W. (1971). Dictation as a device for testing foreign language proficiency. English Language Teaching 25, 254-259; Oller, J. W. & Streiff, V. (1975). Dictation: A test of grammar-based expectancies. ELT Journal 30(1).
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.relevance: Script-practice dictation judges aural form recognition plus orthographic (spelling or script) form recall, and in sentences, grammar. It is good evidence for Hear and for the script skill, and partial evidence for Write (typing). Critics (Lado 1956; Morrow 1979) question whether it shows communicative use. The URL is a reference list; I read these claims in secondary sources.

claims.claim: No validation study of jumbled-word sentence rearrangement as a measure of L2 grammar or vocabulary was found. The closest evidence is that elicited-imitation reconstruction involves working memory, comprehension and syntax, and taps implicit or explicit knowledge depending on time pressure. A word-order test predicted L2 Chinese reading better than grammaticality judgment or correction.
claims.source: Inference from related tasks. Lab vs web-based elicited imitation study, Studies in Second Language Acquisition (2024) (authors not recorded).
claims.relevance: Treat rearrange as primarily syntax (sentence or grammar ability) plus written form recognition of the words on the tiles. Give it only a small update to individual words' Write schedules, and none to Say or Hear, unless audio is played. Several orders may be correct, so scoring must accept them all.

claims.claim: No study was found that reports a correlation between spoken and written form recall (saying versus typing the word from its meaning) for the same L2 learners. Related work shows that oral and written production give different lexical profiles from the same learners.
claims.source: No direct source found. Son (2022) is adjacent: picture description in speech and writing, 86 learners.
claims.relevance: The speak question taps phonological form recall plus articulation, graded by speech recognition, which adds error. By the Laufer and Goldstein hierarchy, a correct speak implies meaning recognition and recall strongly. Its link to Write (typing) and Hear is unknown, so use a moderate, not high, weight. This is inference.

gaps: WebFetch and direct HTTP failed (DNS errors and proxy 403), so no paper or abstract page could be opened. Every 'Medium' claim rests on search-engine summaries of abstracts or citing papers. Only Schmitt, Nation & Kremmel 2020 and Steinel et al. 2007 had abstract text quoted closely enough for High.

Milton & Hopkins (2006) r = .68 is a between-learner correlation of yes/no recognition size scores, not a per-word transfer rate. I found no study that reports per-word conditional transfer, i.e. P(know in skill B | correct in skill A), which is what the cross-skill update actually needs.
No direct evidence on how well speaking (oral form recall) and typing (written form recall) agree for the same words and learners. No evidence was found on ASR-graded speaking as a measure.
No validation study of rearrange (jumbled-word) items as a vocabulary or grammar measure.
No validation evidence was found for self-rated reveal (self-scored meaning recall); the yes/no checklist literature on overclaiming, with pseudowords, may be relevant but was not searched.

I did not retrieve McLean, Kramer & Beglar (2015) Listening Vocabulary Levels Test figures (Language Teaching Research 19(6), 741-760, DOI 10.1177/1362168814567889). I did not retrieve Read (2000) on cloze or Schneider, Healy & Bourne (2002) and Griffin & Harley on translation-direction transfer.

Most evidence comes from English as the L2 and from Japanese, Arabic, Greek, Spanish, Chinese, Dutch or Hebrew L1 learners. None comes from Indic target languages or learners of new scripts, where the gap between aural and written knowledge may be larger, as the Arabic-learner result suggests.
Exact correlations among the four modalities were not retrieved: González-Fernández & Schmitt (2020) inter-component r values, and the Laufer & Goldstein correlation matrix.

checked.source: Laufer, B. & Goldstein, Z. (2004). Language Learning 54(3), 399-436.

checked.source: González-Fernández, B. & Schmitt, N. (2020). Applied Linguistics 41(4), 481-505.

checked.source: Psychological Bulletin 144(7), 710-756.
checked.correction: Not verified: no network access. From memory the overall d of about 0.40 and the 192 effect sizes look right. The 0.28, 0.58 and 0.23 subgroup figures are unchecked, and the claim's own 'numbers' field describes the 0.23 inconsistently (once as elaborated retrieval practice, once as elaborated feedback). Check those figures against the paper before using them for weights.

checked.claim: Kang, McDermott & Roediger (2007): without feedback, MC helped more; with feedback, short answer gave the best final performance.
checked.source: European Journal of Cognitive Psychology 19(4-5), 528-558.
checked.correction: Not verified: no network access. From memory the citation and the pattern (feedback flips the advantage to short answer) look right, and the materials were psychology journal articles. No numbers are available.

checked.claim: Rational-deletion cloze is predicted by vocabulary and grammar (Thai EFL 2015, N=104; McKamey 2006, N=48; 2022 think-aloud, N=16).
checked.source: Veridian E-Journal 2015 (no author given); McKamey 2006, Second Language Studies (University of Hawai'i).
checked.correction: Not verified: the site would not resolve. The 2015 study has no author, and the 2022 think-aloud has no source at all. The claim admits these are not peer-reviewed or top-tier sources, so they fail the task's sourcing rule as cited.

checked.claim: Oller (1971) and Oller & Streiff (1975): dictation taps general processing, and correlated best with the total score in the UCLA placement battery and highly with cloze.
checked.source: English Language Teaching 25, 254-259; ELT Journal 30(1).
checked.correction: Not verified: no network access, and the URL is a reference list. From memory the citations exist, with Oller & Streiff at ELT Journal 30(1), about pp. 25-36. No numbers are available, and the claims were read secondhand.

checked.claim: No validation study of jumbled-sentence rearrangement was found; the evidence comes from elicited imitation and a word-order test in L2 Chinese.
checked.source: Inference; unnamed SSLA 2024 elicited-imitation study.
checked.correction: Not verified, and the cited study has no authors. The 'L2 Chinese word-order test' has no source at all. The weights proposed for rearrange are inference only.

checked.claim: No study correlates spoken and written form recall for the same L2 learners; Son (2022) is the nearest related work.
checked.source: Son (2022), SeoulTech repository.
checked.correction: Not verified: no network access. A claim that no study exists cannot be confirmed without searching. Son (2022) is cited without its venue, and the proposed Say-to-Write weight is inference.

claims.claim: Retrieval practice transfers to tests that differ from the practice test. Against a re-exposure (restudy) control, the overall random-effects transfer effect is d = 0.40.
claims.source: Pan, S. C., & Rickard, T. C. (2018). Transfer of test-enhanced learning: Meta-analytic review and synthesis. Psychological Bulletin, 144(7), 710-756
claims.numbers: d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.31, 0.50]; 192 transfer effect sizes from 122 experiments (67 published and unpublished studies, about 10,000 participants). One secondary source lists a weighted mean of 0.49, which conflicts with 0.40.
claims.population: Mixed. Mostly adult and student samples across many materials, not specific to L2.
claims.relevance: This is the general ceiling for partial credit. A success on a different format is worth about half the direct testing effect, not the whole of it (testing effects on identical tests are typically larger; see the gaps). It supports a weight below 1 for cross-skill credit.

claims.claim: Response congruency is the strongest moderator. When the final test asks for the same response as the practice test, transfer is much larger than when the response differs.
claims.source: Pan & Rickard 2018, Psychological Bulletin 144(7), moderator analysis (as quoted in secondary summaries)
claims.numbers: No response congruency: d = 0.28. Congruent responses: +0.30, about d = 0.58. Elaborated retrieval practice: +0.23. Higher initial-test accuracy predicts more transfer.
claims.relevance: Fluenough mapping: chooseMeaning, hearMeaning and hear-and-type-meaning all retrieve the same response (the meaning). They should give each other large credit (Recognition and Hear, d about 0.58). Say and Write retrieve the L2 form instead, so credit flowing from Recognition or Hear to them should be smaller (d about 0.28). The initial-accuracy moderator means only successful answers should transfer credit; failures should not.

claims.claim: Transfer is greatest across test formats (for example free recall to multiple choice on the same information) and weakest for rearranged stimulus-response items (cue and target swapped) and for untested material seen only at study.
claims.source: Pan & Rickard 2018, Psychological Bulletin 144(7)
claims.numbers: Across formats: d = 0.58 (secondary notes). Untested material seen during study: d = 0.16, p = .20, k = 17 (not significant). I did not find a category-specific d for rearrangement.
claims.relevance: Same direction, different format (choose versus type, MCQ versus cloze, recognition reveal versus chooseMeaning) deserves near-full credit. Reversing direction (meaning to word versus word to meaning: Recognition versus Write or Say) is the weakest case. Words shown only as distractors or in a passage should get almost no credit.

claims.claim: Testing enhances transfer across temporal contexts, test formats and knowledge domains; the small but growing literature reports robust benefits of testing on transfer.
claims.source: Carpenter, S. K. (2012). Testing enhances the transfer of learning. Current Directions in Psychological Science, 21(5), 279-283
claims.numbers: Narrative review with no pooled effect size
claims.relevance: Qualitative support for letting one question type update other formats of the same skill, and for some cross-skill credit

claims.claim: Testing the forward direction of a pair (cue to target) also improves later recall in the backward direction (target to cue) compared with restudy: the 'backward transfer effect'. A later source notes it had been shown only with simple native-language word pairs.
claims.source: Carpenter, S. K., Pashler, H., & Vul, E. (2006). What types of learning are enhanced by a cued recall test? Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 13(5), 826-830 (citation from memory, described by a later paper)
claims.numbers: Not found
claims.population: Adult English speakers; L1 word pairs
claims.relevance: Direct evidence that a Recognition success (L2 to L1) should give partial credit to Write or Say (L1 to L2), and vice versa, but less than a same-direction review. The DOI comes from memory and needs checking.

claims.claim: Associative symmetry: in paired-associate memory, accuracy on forward and backward probes of the same pair is very highly correlated, nearly as high as two probes in the same direction. The fitted forward-backward storage correlation was close to 1.0. Symmetry weakens to mid-range correlations in other paradigms (Caplan 2005, 19-word lists), and for semantically related pairs the two directions can be modified separately.
claims.source: Rizzuto, D. S., & Kahana, M. J. (2001). An autoassociative neural network model of paired-associate learning. Neural Computation, 13, 2075-2092; Kahana, M. J. (2002). Associative symmetry and memory theory. Memory & Cognition, 30(6), 823-840
claims.numbers: Forward-backward correlation parameter close to 1.0 for all participants (model fit). Caplan 2005: mid-range values.
claims.population: Adult native speakers; L1 word pairs
claims.relevance: The two directions largely share one memory trace in strength, which argues for strong coupling of Recognition and Write or Say stability. The L2 evidence below shows direction still matters for what is learned (form versus meaning), so the coupling is strong but well below 1.

claims.claim: Learning direction determines what gets better. On a production test, L1-to-L2 (productive) learners had a sizable advantage over L2-to-L1 (receptive) learners. On recognition, receptive learners did better. Testing was immediate and after 3 weeks.
claims.source: Steinel, M. P., Hulstijn, J. H., & Steinel, W. (2007). Second language idiom learning in a paired-associate paradigm: Effects of direction of learning, direction of testing, idiom imageability, and idiom transparency. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 29, 449-484
claims.numbers: n = 129, 20 idioms. Exact effect sizes not retrieved.
claims.population: Dutch university students learning English L2 idioms
claims.relevance: Credit across directions is asymmetric and less than full. Practice in a direction helps that same direction most.

claims.claim: Productive learning of word pairs gave larger gains than receptive learning on receptive and productive orthography, and on productive meaning, syntax and grammatical functions. Receptive learning gave larger gains only on receptive knowledge of meaning. If only one method is used, productive learning may be more effective.
claims.source: Webb, S. (2009). The effects of receptive and productive learning of word pairs on vocabulary knowledge. RELC Journal, 40(3), 360-376
claims.numbers: MANOVA over 10 measures: F(10,51) = 3.73, p < .001 (from an auto-summary; verify). Exact gains not retrieved.
claims.population: Japanese EFL learners (84 per abstract summary)
claims.relevance: Asymmetric transfer. A Write or Say success (production) should give more credit to Recognition than a Recognition success gives to Write or Say. Production largely implies reception, but not the reverse.

claims.claim: Webb (2005) found the opposite pattern when time on task was equalised: receptive learning (glossed sentences) produced greater receptive and productive knowledge than a sentence-production task.
claims.source: Webb, S. (2005). Receptive and productive vocabulary learning: The effects of reading and writing on word knowledge. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 27(1), 33-52
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.relevance: The size of production-to-reception transfer depends on task and time. It cautions against hard-coding a large asymmetric weight without in-app calibration.

claims.claim: Productive learning was more beneficial for learning the form and receptive learning for learning the meaning. Learners did best when the test direction matched the study direction.
claims.source: Mondria, J.-A., & Wiersma, B. (2004). Receptive, productive, and receptive + productive L2 vocabulary learning: What difference does it make? In P. Bogaards & B. Laufer (Eds.), Vocabulary in a Second Language (pp. 79-100). John Benjamins
claims.numbers: From a secondary summary: word-list learners gained 53% on immediate form recall and 12% on delayed form recall after 13 days. Results for the receptive + productive condition not found.
claims.population: Dutch secondary-school learners of French (population inferred, not verified)
claims.relevance: Supports a same-direction-is-best rule: the full review applies to the practised skill, and only partial credit to the other direction.

claims.claim: Training L1 cue to L2 response (productive direction) gave better retention on both comprehension and production tests than the easier L2-to-L1 direction. Receptive test scores were higher than productive scores whatever the learning direction.
claims.source: Griffin, G., & Harley, T. A. (1996). List learning of second language vocabulary. Applied Psycholinguistics, 17, 443-460
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.population: English secondary-school learners of French aged 11-13 (from Griffin's 1992 thesis; journal sample not verified)
claims.relevance: A production success implies a recognition success more strongly than the reverse. This supports larger credit from Write or Say to Recognition or Hear than the other way. The DOI comes from memory and needs checking.

claims.claim: The harder English-to-French direction during learning produced higher accuracy on the 1-week retention test and somewhat higher relearning accuracy, regardless of which direction was used at relearning. Difficulty aided both retention and transfer to the other task. A 2025 six-experiment follow-up found difficult conditions hurt during learning and immediate testing but made no difference or helped at relearning and delayed testing.
claims.source: Schneider, V. I., Healy, A. F., & Bourne, L. E., Jr. (2002). What is learned under difficult conditions is hard to forget: Contextual interference effects in foreign vocabulary acquisition, retention, and transfer. Journal of Memory and Language, 46, 419-440; Healy, Schneider & Kole (2025), Behavioral Sciences 15(5), 692
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.population: English-speaking US undergraduates learning French vocabulary
claims.relevance: A productive (L1-to-L2) success transfers to relearning in the receptive direction too. It supports giving Recognition credit for Write or Say successes, and giving productive successes more weight as evidence of durable knowledge.

claims.claim: The better learning direction depends on proficiency. For lower-proficiency learners, L2-to-L1 retrieval practice was more effective; for higher-proficiency learners, L1-to-L2 was more effective. Earlier studies comparing directions are inconsistent.
claims.source: Terai, M., Yamashita, J., & Pasich, K. E. (2021). Effects of learning direction in retrieval practice on EFL vocabulary learning. Studies in Second Language Acquisition, 43(5)
claims.numbers: Not retrieved
claims.relevance: The cross-skill weight could be conditioned on the learner's Elo ability. Beginners get more from receptive success, so do not over-credit early receptive-only learners in production. The DOI comes from memory and needs checking.

claims.claim: For productive knowledge of spelling, recall formats beat recognition. When spelling was not required, recognition formats were the more useful choice, and better performance during learning did not necessarily mean better posttest performance.
claims.source: Nakata, T. (2016). Effects of retrieval formats on second language vocabulary learning. International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching, 54(3), 257-289
claims.numbers: N = 64, 60 Swahili-English pairs, 4 conditions. Effect sizes not retrieved.
claims.population: English-speaking college students learning Swahili words
claims.relevance: Choose-type questions (chooseWord, MCQ cloze) do not imply typed-form knowledge. A chooseWord success should give only partial credit to type-the-word or Write-typed, while a typed success largely implies the choose form. This argues for a separate typed-form strength or a lower weight for choose-to-type.

claims.claim: Testing a subset of prose material improved recall of related untested material 24 hours later ('retrieval-induced facilitation'). Extra study time without a test did not produce the benefit. A 2010 follow-up found the benefit grows from 20 minutes to 24 hours and then levels off.
claims.source: Chan, J. C. K., McDermott, K. B., & Roediger, H. L. (2006). Retrieval-induced facilitation: Initially nontested material can benefit from prior testing of related material. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General, 135(4), 553-571
claims.numbers: 3 experiments, N = 210. Effect sizes not retrieved.
claims.relevance: Partial support for crediting a word's other skills, or related words, after a success, mainly for integrated or coherent material. Pan & Rickard's pooled estimate for untested items (d = 0.16, n.s.) says this credit should be small.

claims.claim: Testing with keyword mediators beat restudy-only by almost three times on a one-week final test. Keywords were remembered more often after test-restudy (51%) than after restudy only (34%).
claims.source: Pyc, M. A., & Rawson, K. A. (2010). Why testing improves memory: Mediator effectiveness hypothesis. Science, 330(6002), 335
claims.numbers: N = 118, 48 Swahili-English pairs. Mediator recall 51% vs 34%. Final-test performance about 3x restudy.
claims.relevance: Shows why an L2-to-L1 test can help other directions: it strengthens a shared mediator. It supports partial cross-direction credit.

claims.claim: Retrieval practice beat imitation (repeating after a model) for foreign vocabulary learning, measured on comprehension and production or pronunciation.
claims.source: Kang, S. H. K., Gollan, T. H., & Pashler, H. (2013). Don't just repeat after me: Retrieval practice is better than imitation for foreign vocabulary learning. Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 20(6), 1259-1265
claims.numbers: Not retrieved; the direction of the result is inferred from the title
claims.relevance: A Say item answered from the meaning, without a model to copy, is a real retrieval and should count as a review. A shadowing or read-aloud item should count little toward FSRS.

claims.claim: Mode of input changes which word knowledge develops. Reading while listening gave more spoken-form recall (picture naming) than listening only. Groups that heard the words (reading while listening, listening only) were rated less accented and more comprehensible than the reading-only group. Sound-spelling consistency also moderated results.
claims.source: Uchihara, T., Webb, S., Saito, K., & Trofimovich, P. (2022). Does mode of input affect how second language learners create form-meaning connections and pronounce second language words? The Modern Language Journal
claims.numbers: N = 75, 40 low-frequency words. Tests at pretest, immediately after, and about 6 days later. Effect sizes not retrieved.
claims.relevance: Written-only practice transfers only partially to spoken skills. A Recognition or Write success should give the Say skill reduced credit, and should not credit Say pronunciation quality at all. Credit to Say or Hear from written skills should be lower in scripts with low sound-spelling consistency.

claims.claim: The modality of video input (audio, captions, or both) affected learning of written versus aural word forms. The captioned groups (audio plus captions, and captions only) scored higher on written-form tests.
claims.source: Sydorenko, T. (2010). Modality of input and vocabulary acquisition. Language Learning & Technology, 14(2), 50-73
claims.numbers: Groups: VAC n = 8, VA n = 9, VC n = 9 (N = 26). Aural-form results not retrieved.
claims.relevance: Written and aural form knowledge develop partly separately, so Hear and Recognition (written) should be coupled, not merged

claims.claim: Aural (phonological) and written (orthographic) vocabulary sizes are related but distinct. The 0.68 coupling weight Fluenough uses comes from this paper.
claims.source: Milton, J., & Hopkins, N. (2006). Comparing phonological and orthographic vocabulary size: Do vocabulary tests underestimate the knowledge of some learners? Canadian Modern Language Review, 63(1), 127-147
claims.numbers: I could not verify the correlation value (.68) in this session
claims.population: L2 English learners (Arabic and Greek L1 per later citations; not verified)
claims.relevance: A between-learner correlation of vocabulary sizes is evidence for coupling the ability (Elo) layer. It is not a measure of how much one review strengthens memory in another skill, so it should not be reused unchanged as the FSRS review-credit weight.

claims.claim: Proposed quantification, inferred from the claims above and not reported by any single study. Same skill, different format: about 0.8-1.0 of a review. Same direction and same response, different channel (Recognition and Hear): about 0.5-0.6. Production success to reception (Write or Say to Recognition or Hear): about 0.5. Reception success to production: about 0.25-0.3. Choose-form to typed-form: about 0.3-0.5. Untested distractors or related words: about 0-0.15. Failures give no credit to other skills.
claims.source: Inference from Pan & Rickard 2018 (d 0.28 vs 0.58 vs untested 0.16, against a direct testing effect of roughly d 0.5-0.8 in other meta-analyses, not retrieved here), Webb 2009, Griffin & Harley 1996, Steinel et al. 2007, Nakata 2016, Uchihara et al. 2022
claims.numbers: Ratios such as 0.28/0.58 ≈ 0.48 of the congruent-transfer effect
claims.relevance: In FSRS, implement this as a fractional stability update, or a partial review, on the other skills' schedules. Do not reset their due dates. Calibrate the weights later from Fluenough's own review logs: how a success in skill A predicts the next answer in skill B.

gaps: WebFetch and direct downloads were blocked in this session (DNS failure or the proxy refused the connection for pubmed, cambridge.org, researchgate and retrievalpractice.org). No full text or abstract page could be opened. Every claim comes from search-engine extracts of abstracts or secondary summaries. 'High' is used only where the search extract reproduced the abstract's own statements.

Pan & Rickard 2018: the category-specific d for rearranged stimulus-response items (direction reversal) was not retrieved. Check the paper's moderator tables (sc-pan.github.io/pdf/PR_2018W.pdf hosts a preprint).
The Milton & Hopkins (2006) correlation value used by the app (.68) could not be confirmed. It is a between-learner size correlation, not a within-learner review-transfer rate.

Exact effect sizes were not found for: Griffin & Harley 1996, Mondria & Wiersma 2004 (including the receptive+productive condition), Webb 2009 per-measure gains, Schneider et al. 2002 direction effects, Kang et al. 2013, Carpenter et al. 2006 backward-transfer size, Sydorenko 2010 aural results, Uchihara et al. 2022.

No study found reports a 'transfer rate' in FSRS or stability terms (for example: one review in skill A equals x reviews in skill B). Any numeric cross-skill weight must be inferred, and should then be fitted on the app's own review logs.

No direct evidence was found on speaking-practice (ASR-graded) transfer to listening or reading, on dictation or script practice transferring to word skills, or on whether grammar-form practice credits lexical skills.

DOIs given from memory and not confirmed in this session: Carpenter, Pashler & Vul 2006; Griffin & Harley 1996; Terai et al. 2021; Webb 2005; Pyc & Rawson 2010; Chan et al. 2006. Verify them before citing.
The direct testing effect (same test) used as the denominator in the quantification claim was not retrieved. Rowland 2014 or Adesope et al. 2017 would give it.

checked.claim: Pan & Rickard 2018: retrieval practice transfers to tests that differ from the practice test. Against a re-exposure (restudy) control, the overall random-effects transfer effect is d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.31, 0.50], from 192 effect sizes in 122 experiments (67 articles).
checked.source: Pan, S. C., & Rickard, T. C. (2018). Psychological Bulletin, 144(7), 710-756. DOI 10.1037/bul0000151
checked.correction: The abstract (PubMed 29733621, seen through search snippets) states the figures as claimed: d = 0.40, 95% CI [0.31, 0.50], 192 effect sizes, 122 experiments, 67 published and unpublished articles. The exact N is 10,382, not 'about 10,000'. The abstract adds that after publication-bias correction the intercept predictions were 'substantially reduced, often indicating no positive transfer' when none of the moderators were present. I could not trace the 'weighted mean 0.49' figure, so the abstract value 0.40 stands. Caveat: the line 'a success on a different format is worth about half the direct testing effect' is the researcher's inference, not a finding of the paper. Confidence: High for the numbers (abstract wording returned by search). Network limits blocked fetching the PDF directly.

checked.claim: Response congruency is the strongest moderator: no congruency d = 0.28; congruent about d = 0.58 (+0.30); elaborated retrieval practice +0.23; higher initial-test accuracy predicts more transfer.
checked.source: Pan & Rickard 2018, moderator analysis (via secondary summary)
checked.correction: Only the qualitative part is in the abstract: response congruency, elaborated retrieval practice and initial test performance 'strongly influence the likelihood of positive transfer'. The numbers (0.28, +0.30 giving about 0.58, +0.23, and about +0.0058 d per percentage point of initial accuracy) come only from a secondary note (Matuschak's notes) and a 2025 citing paper. I could not check them against the paper's tables. Confidence stays Medium. The step from 'initial accuracy' to 'only successes should transfer credit' is an inference. The moderator concerns accuracy at the level of a whole study, not individual items.

checked.claim: Transfer is greatest across test formats and weakest for rearranged stimulus-response items and for untested material seen at study. Across formats d = 0.58; untested material d = 0.16, p = .20, k = 17.
checked.source: Pan & Rickard 2018
checked.correction: The abstract confirms the ranking. Transfer was greatest across test formats, to application and inference questions, to medical-diagnosis problems, and to mediator and related-word cues. It was weakest to rearranged stimulus-response items, to untested materials seen during initial study, and to worked-example problems. The figure 'across formats d = 0.58' is not supported. The secondary notes give 0.58 as the congruent-response estimate, and the claim appears to merge the two. The figure d = 0.16, p = .20, k = 17 for untested material is quoted by Glaser & Richter (2025, Teaching of Psychology, doi 10.1177/00986283231218943), which cites Pan & Rickard. I did not check it in the primary paper, so confidence is Medium. No category-specific d for rearranged items was found.

checked.claim: Carpenter 2012: testing enhances transfer across temporal contexts, test formats and knowledge domains, with robust benefits in a small but growing literature.
checked.source: Carpenter, S. K. (2012). Current Directions in Psychological Science, 21(5), 279-283
checked.correction: The abstract (paraphrased in search results) reviews research on how testing affects transfer across temporal contexts, test formats and knowledge domains, and says the small but growing literature shows robust benefits. It is a narrative review with no pooled effect size. The citation details and DOI are correct.

checked.claim: Testing forward (cue to target) improves later backward recall (target to cue) compared with restudy: the backward transfer effect. A later source says it had been shown only with native-language word pairs.
checked.source: Carpenter, S. K., Pashler, H., & Vul, E. (2006). Psychonomic Bulletin & Review, 13(5), 826-830
checked.correction: The paper exists as cited: title, authors, PB&R volume 13, pages 826-830. Citing sources describe its finding as substantial transfer to the reversed, untested direction on a delayed final test. I did not see the DOI 10.3758/BF03194004 in any source, so it remains unverified. The 'only native-language pairs' statement is incomplete. The same later source says the effect has been shown with simple native-language pairs (Carpenter et al. 2006; Cheng 2014; Rickard & Pan 2020) and with native-foreign pairs (Barenberg et al. 2021). That makes it more relevant to L2 than the claim suggests. No effect sizes were retrieved. Confidence: Medium (secondary descriptions).

checked.claim: Associative symmetry: forward and backward probes are very highly correlated, and the fitted forward-backward storage correlation is close to 1.0. Symmetry weakens to mid-range correlations in other paradigms (Caplan 2005, 19-word lists). For semantically related pairs the two directions can be modified separately.
checked.source: Rizzuto & Kahana (2001) Neural Computation 13, 2075-2092; Kahana (2002) Memory & Cognition 30(6), 823-840
checked.correction: Rizzuto & Kahana 2001 is confirmed. The abstract says the model fits significantly better when forward and backward storage strengths are highly correlated, and it favours a single blended unit over separately modifiable associations. 'Close to 1.0 for all participants' is how Aenugu & Huber (2021, Neural Computation 33(12)) describe the result; it is not quoted from the 2001 abstract. Kahana 2002 exists as cited. The Caplan 2005 detail is unsupported. Caplan 2005 (J. Math. Psych. 49, 383-402) is 'Associative isolation', and I found no '19-word list, mid-range correlation' result. The closest support is Caplan, Glaholt & McIntosh (2006, JEP:LMC 32(6)): forward and backward probes were highly correlated for pairs and less so for triples. Kahana & Caplan (2002) found a forward-recall advantage for triples and serial lists. The claim about semantically related pairs is unsupported because no source was found.

checked.claim: Steinel et al. 2007: productive (L1 to L2) learners had a sizable advantage on production tests and receptive learners did better on recognition. Testing was immediate and after 3 weeks. n = 129, 20 idioms, Dutch university students.
checked.source: Steinel, M. P., Hulstijn, J. H., & Steinel, W. (2007). SSLA 29, 449-484
checked.correction: The abstract (Leiden open-access copy, hdl 1887/14200) confirms n = 129 Dutch university students, 20 English idioms, receptive or productive learning, tests in both directions immediately and after 3 weeks. Productive learners had a 'sizable advantage' on the productive test, and receptive learners did better on recognition. No effect sizes were retrieved. The DOI is given as 10.1017/S0272263107070271 in the search result, which I did not resolve independently.

checked.claim: Webb 2009: productive learning of word pairs gave larger gains on most measures, receptive learning only on receptive meaning, and if only one method is used productive learning may be more effective. MANOVA F(10,51) = 3.73.
checked.source: Webb, S. (2009). RELC Journal, 40(3), 360-376
checked.correction: The abstract (ERIC EJ865637) confirms Japanese EFL students, five aspects each tested receptively and productively, larger receptive-meaning gains from receptive learning, and 'if only one method is used, productive learning of word pairs might be more effective'. The exact set of aspects where productive learning won could not be checked against the full text. One citing review lists productive orthography, meaning, association, syntax and grammar, plus receptive orthography and meaning. That conflicts with the claim's 'receptive learning larger only on receptive meaning' if receptive meaning is included. The MANOVA F(10,51) = 3.73 and n = 84 were not verified. Treat them as unsupported until the full text is read.

checked.claim: Webb 2005: with time on task equalised, receptive learning (glossed sentences) produced greater receptive and productive knowledge than sentence production, which is the opposite of Webb 2009.
checked.correction: The abstract says that with equal time on both tasks the reading (glossed-sentence) task was superior (Experiment 1). When time depended on what each task needed to complete, so that writing took longer, the writing task was more effective (Experiment 2). Webb concludes that if Experiment 2 reflects authentic learning, the case for productive tasks is stronger. So 'opposite pattern' holds only under equal time, and the paper's own conclusion leans toward productive tasks. The detail 'greater receptive and productive knowledge' was not confirmed beyond 'reading task was superior'.

checked.claim: Mondria & Wiersma 2004: productive learning better for form, receptive better for meaning, and learners best when test direction matched study direction. Word-list learners gained 53% on immediate form recall and 12% on delayed recall after 13 days.
checked.source: Mondria & Wiersma (2004), in Bogaards & Laufer (Eds.), Vocabulary in a Second Language, pp. 79-100, John Benjamins
checked.correction: The chapter exists as cited (DOI 10.1075/lllt.10.08mon; Groningen portal; Dutch version in Levende Talen Tijdschrift 2004). I found no abstract or summary that states its findings. Citing papers use it only for 'productive knowledge is acquired more slowly and is more susceptible to forgetting'. The 53% and 12% (13 days) figures were not found anywhere. Population is unverified.

checked.claim: Griffin & Harley 1996: L1-to-L2 training gave better retention on both comprehension and production tests than L2-to-L1. Receptive scores were higher than productive whatever the direction. Learners were English school learners of French aged 11-13.
checked.source: Griffin, G., & Harley, T. A. (1996). Applied Psycholinguistics, 17, 443-460
checked.correction: The paper exists (Applied Psycholinguistics 17(4), 443-460; Cambridge). The abstract reports a study of comprehensive-school pupils aged 11-13 learning French. Its conclusion is narrower than claimed: L1-L2 presentation was 'the more versatile form of presentation if both production and comprehension of L2 items were required'. 'Better retention on both tests' and 'receptive scores higher than productive regardless of direction' were not verified. The DOI 10.1017/S0142716400008195 was not seen in any result and is unverified.

checked.claim: Schneider, Healy & Bourne 2002: the harder English-to-French direction produced higher 1-week retention and somewhat higher relearning accuracy regardless of relearning direction. Healy, Schneider & Kole 2025 (6 experiments): difficulty hurt during learning and immediate testing but made no difference or helped at relearning and delayed testing.
checked.source: Schneider, Healy & Bourne (2002) JML 46, 419-440; Healy, Schneider & Kole (2025) Behavioral Sciences 15(5), 692
checked.correction: Healy et al. 2025 (doi 10.3390/bs15050692, PMC12108878) confirms the six-experiment summary: four earlier and two new experiments, French-English pairs, with difficult conditions at a disadvantage during learning and immediate testing and no difference or an advantage at relearning and delayed testing. It also concludes that harder initial learning 'does not always lead to superior retention', which the claim leaves out. The 2002 result ('more accurate on the 1-week retention test, somewhat more accurate during relearning, regardless of direction at relearning') comes from Healy et al. 2025's description of it, not the 2002 abstract, so confidence is Medium. Participants were native English speakers with no prior French who typed responses.

checked.claim: Terai, Yamashita & Pasich 2021: L2-to-L1 retrieval was more effective for lower-proficiency learners and L1-to-L2 for higher-proficiency learners. Earlier studies are inconsistent.
checked.source: Terai, M., Yamashita, J., & Pasich, K. E. (2021). SSLA 43(5)
checked.correction: The ERIC record (EJ1319303) and abstract confirm the finding and the DOI 10.1017/S0272263121000346. Details: SSLA 43(5), 1116-1137. N = 28 native Japanese speakers learning English, which is a small sample. A minor erratum (a misspelled name in the running head) was issued.

checked.claim: Nakata 2016: recall formats beat recognition for productive spelling knowledge, recognition is preferable when spelling is not required, and better learning-phase performance did not mean better posttest performance. N = 64, 60 Swahili-English pairs, 4 conditions.
checked.correction: The abstract (researchmap listing) confirms 64 English-speaking college students, 60 Swahili-English pairs, flashcard software, and four conditions (recognition, recall, hybrid, productive recall only). It also confirms recall over recognition for productive spelling and recognition as more useful when spelling is not required. The 'learning-phase versus posttest' point is supported by the thesis summary: productive recall 'may decrease learning phase performance'. No effect sizes were retrieved. The DOI 10.1515/iral-2015-0022 matches.

checked.claim: Chan, McDermott & Roediger 2006: testing part of prose material improved recall of related untested material 24 h later, and extra study without testing did not. N = 210, 3 experiments. A 2010 follow-up found the benefit grows from 20 min to 24 h and then levels off.
checked.source: Chan, McDermott & Roediger (2006). JEP: General, 135(4), 553-571
checked.correction: The abstract confirms 3 experiments, N = 210, prose materials, facilitation at 24 h, and no facilitation from additional study without testing. Experiment 3 showed that conscious strategies can modulate the effect. The follow-up is Chan, J. C. K. (2010), Memory, 18(1), 49-57 (doi 10.1080/09658210903405737). Its abstract says the effect grows between 20 min and 24 h and levels off between 24 h and 7 days. Note also Oliva & Storm (2022, PMC9425789): the effect replicated but was 'somewhat smaller than previously observed', and Chan (2009) ties it to well-integrated material.

checked.claim: Pyc & Rawson 2010: testing with keyword mediators beat restudy-only by almost three times on a one-week final test, and keywords were remembered more often after test-restudy (51%) than restudy (34%). N = 118, 48 Swahili-English pairs.
checked.source: Pyc, M. A., & Rawson, K. A. (2010). Science, 330(6002), 335
checked.correction: The citation exists (PubMed 20947756). Supported: test-restudy produced mediators that were more likely to be retrieved and more likely to elicit targets. Mediator recall at final test was 51% after test-restudy versus 34% after restudy, according to a citing paper and press coverage. When mediators were supplied at test, recall improved after restudy but not after test-restudy. The 'almost three times' final-test advantage was not found in any source and is unsupported. N = 118, 48 pairs, the one-week delay and the Swahili materials were not verified by the sources I reached.

checked.claim: Kang, Gollan & Pashler 2013: retrieval practice beat imitation for foreign vocabulary, measured on comprehension and production or pronunciation. US undergraduates, Hebrew words.
checked.source: Kang, Gollan & Pashler (2013). PB&R, 20(6), 1259-1265
checked.correction: The citation and DOI are confirmed. Two experiments: US undergraduates learned 40 Hebrew nouns over 3 or 6 cycles. A summary of the abstract (Semantic Scholar) reports that retrieval practice gave better comprehension and production with no loss of pronunciation quality. Pronunciation was therefore not better, only no worse. Confidence rises from Low to Medium because the source is a secondary summary, not the verbatim abstract.

checked.claim: Uchihara et al. 2022: reading-while-listening gave more spoken-form recall than listening-only. Groups that heard the words were less accented and more comprehensible than reading-only. Sound-spelling consistency moderated results. N = 75, 40 words, tests about 6 days later.
checked.source: Uchihara, Webb, Saito & Trofimovich (2022). The Modern Language Journal
checked.correction: The abstract confirms all of the claim: 75 Japanese EFL learners, 3 conditions, 40 low-frequency words with pictures, picture naming at pretest, immediately after and about 6 days later. It adds that only spoken input without spelling (listening-only) retained the more target-like accent over time. The authors conclude that simultaneous written and spoken input is best for form-meaning connections and comprehensibility.

checked.claim: Sydorenko 2010: input modality affected learning of written versus aural forms, and the captioned groups scored higher on written-form tests. VAC n = 8, VA n = 9, VC n = 9.
checked.source: Sydorenko, T. (2010). Language Learning & Technology, 14(2), 50-73
checked.correction: Confirmed: 26 second-semester learners of Russian with the group sizes as stated. Captioned groups did better on written than aural recognition. The VA (no-caption) group showed the reverse pattern, better aural than written, and VAC learned more meanings than VA. This supports keeping written and aural forms separate.

checked.claim: Milton & Hopkins 2006: aural and written vocabulary sizes are related but distinct, and the 0.68 coupling weight comes from this paper.
checked.source: Milton, J., & Hopkins, N. (2006). Canadian Modern Language Review, 63(1), 127-147
checked.correction: The citation and DOI are confirmed. Later citing papers report a correlation of 0.68 between Aural Lex (phonological) and X-Lex (orthographic) scores in 126 learners of English (38 Arabic L1, 88 Greek L1). Arabic speakers had a nearly balanced aural and written lexicon, while Greek speakers knew more words in writing. Both tests are yes/no recognition checklists. I found the figure only in secondary sources (Medium), not in the primary text. The researcher's caveat stands: this is a correlation between learners, not a measure of transfer between skills within one learner.

checked.claim: Proposed weights: same skill different format 0.8-1.0; Recognition and Hear 0.5-0.6; production to reception 0.5; reception to production 0.25-0.3; choose to type 0.3-0.5; untested 0-0.15; failures give no credit.
checked.source: Inference from Pan & Rickard 2018 and the L2 studies above
checked.correction: No study reports these weights. They are an inference, labelled Low. Two inputs are weaker than presented. First, 0.58 is the congruent-response moderator estimate from a secondary summary, not an 'across formats' value. Second, the untested d = 0.16 comes from a secondary citation. The direction of asymmetry (production implies reception more than the reverse) is supported by Webb 2009, Steinel et al. 2007 and Griffin & Harley 1996. It is contradicted under equal time by Webb 2005 (Exp. 1) and depends on proficiency (Terai et al. 2021). That supports the researcher's recommendation to calibrate from Fluenough's own review logs rather than hard-coding the weights.
